chapters.question_prompt: What do the IICRC S500 and S520 standards require for water damage restoration and mold remediation, and how do practitioners get certified?
chapters.title: Working to the Standard: IICRC S500 Water Damage and S520 Mold Remediation
chapters.subtitle: S500 2021 edition changes, S520 2015 and 2024 revisions, S520 core principles and homeowner guide, the Texas TMARR overlay, applied structural drying readings, and the MRS application and exam handbook
chapters.executive_summary: Working practitioners boil the IICRC standards down to a hard consensus: remove mold physically, never fog or bleach it, and judge jobs by Conditions 1, 2 and 3 rather than visible square footage. “Should” is the standard of care, and any deviation needs documentation and written authorization, because courts measure remediators against the book. The street mechanics are specific: 6 mil fire-retardant poly, -5 pascals on a manometer, HEPA at 99.97% at 0.3 microns, a HEPA filter near $153, moisture readings every 5 ft, 12 to 16 air movers for 750 square feet, and the same meter used daily. Disagreements are real: Mark Cornelius says cleaning to zero prices remediation out of the market, Nicole Bijlsma ranks species order over spore counts, and speakers split on whether remediators may test their own work.

key_metrics.label: Containment negative pressure target
key_metrics.context: Balanced Building Biology calls -5 pascals, tracked with a manometer, the crucial metric proving a mold containment is actually working.

key_metrics.label: Air movers for a 750 sq ft loss
key_metrics.metric: Air movers for a 750 sq ft loss
key_metrics.context: Darren Floyd's worked example of the 2015 placement rule: one per room, plus one per 50-70 sq ft of floor, one per 100-150 sq ft of wall/ceiling above 2 ft, and one per offset over 18 in.

key_metrics.label: HEPA filter replacement cost
key_metrics.context: AFD filter stack pricing: pre-filter $8-12, secondary $15-20, HEPA about $153, with HEPA capturing 99.97% at 0.3 µm and carbon filters handling odor.

key_metrics.label: MRS certification fees
key_metrics.context: Mold Remediation Specialist candidates pay $150 on application and $300 after approval; two attempts within 90 days, and failing both means a one-year wait.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every serious voice on the mold side lands on the same rule: the job is physical removal, not chemistry. Phill McGurk calls removal “the big one” among five principles (safety, documentation before, during and after, containment, removal, and fixing the moisture) and says flatly that “proper remediation is about physical removal,” with spraying or fogging “totally inadequate” because dead mold is still an allergen [Dl8DpDk97_A @ 00:03:11]. S520 consensus body chair Jim Pearson pushes the same line for the 2024 edition: remove mold rather than kill it, and vice chair Scott Armor reduces the whole document to “remove don't kill” [JOiWfXdUwjM @ 00:27:50]. Time's Dark Captains reads it straight off the page: S520 4.4 requires physical removal, killing or encapsulating is inadequate, and 5.8.1.1 says chemicals are not a substitute [y00Yi4bnLx4 @ 00:29:33]. The 2015 revision already told remediators not to mist disinfectants or sanitizers “to try to kill mold in lieu of source removal,” and ruled out temperature extremes, hot or cold, as an alternative to cleaning [6CI2NAsooLw @ 00:11:36]. The operator takeaway is blunt: a bid built around a fogger, bleach, or an ozone box is a bid built outside the standard of care, and these practitioners treat it as a red flag rather than a shortcut.

The second point of agreement is how a job gets sized. McGurk calls Condition 1 a normal, not sterile, environment and “the finish line” of every job, Condition 2 the settled or airborne spores and fragments that “amateurs totally missed,” and Condition 3 the “mold factory” that has to come out before the fallout gets cleaned [Dl8DpDk97_A @ 00:01:23]. Balanced Building Biology defines Condition 1 as indoor fungal levels similar to or lower than outdoors, and says Condition 3 includes active, dormant or dead growth [YdUmzaa5wO0 @ 00:00:57]. Pearson notes “air” was added to the Condition definitions in the 2024 edition, so the Conditions now reach airborne material rather than surfaces alone [JOiWfXdUwjM @ 00:26:38]. Time's Dark Captains drives the practical consequence home: Texas TMARR draws its line at 25 contiguous square feet including 2 ft past visible growth, OSHA tiers run under 10, 10 to 30, 30 to 100 and over 100 square feet, but the S520 foreword rejects visible-area thresholds and replaces them with Conditions 1, 2 and 3 [y00Yi4bnLx4 @ 00:15:58]. For an operator, that means a small visible patch does not mean a small job; McGurk's dandelion analogy makes the same point, since the flower is small but the seeds have already spread.

The third consensus is the language and its legal teeth. Darren Floyd of APPALeadership lays out the vocabulary: “shall” is mandatory, “should” is the standard of care, and “recommend,” “may” and “can” are not; a deviation, in Floyd's words, “is not a license to do something wrong,” more like a detour [cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:08:12]. Time's Dark Captains puts it in street terms (under “should” you need a “damn good reason” not to) and spells out the deviation drill from S520 9.3.4: document it, communicate with affected parties, and get written authorization [y00Yi4bnLx4 @ 00:07:28]. Pearson is just as direct: the standard is voluntary, deviation needs written full disclosure to the client, and in front of a judge or jury, not following it means “you're probably going to lose” [JOiWfXdUwjM @ 00:14:53]. Learn To Restore explains where that weight comes from: ANSI accreditation, which arrived with the 2006 edition, does not validate the water-damage content but the drafting procedure, meaning balance of interest, no favoring of any company or person, and every one of thousands of public comments answered, so “it has a lot of legal weight behind it by the time you get there” [i4RGAC2VwaY @ 00:03:38]. None of these speakers treats voluntary as optional once a claim turns into a lawsuit.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Containment is where the numbers get specific. Balanced Building Biology specs 6 mil fire-retardant poly, zip walls and critical barriers over vents and doors, warns never to demolish or place air movers before the room is sealed, and names the crucial metric: hold -5 pascals of negative pressure, tracked with a manometer, using true HEPA at 99.97% filtration at 0.3 microns, while shop vacs and M-class extractors are “not allowed” [YdUmzaa5wO0 @ 00:02:47]. Andrew Melrose runs the same kit on mold jobs: 6 mil plastic, negative air, high-CFM HEPA scrubbers, a dehumidifier to stop humidity spikes, HEPA vacuums, P100 respirators and decon chambers, and names random chemicals, no containment and humidity spikes as the signature of bad work [iQ4PIKW3sEc @ 00:03:54]. Time's Dark Captains adds the Texas poly spec of 4 to 6 mil for walls and ceilings, 10 mil for floors, fire-retardant with flame spread of 25 or less, and reads the standard as not allowing scrubber mode without negative pressure [y00Yi4bnLx4 @ 00:46:31]. Floyd puts the consumables on the P&L: AFD pre-filters run $8 to $12, secondaries $15 to $20, and the HEPA about $153, with carbon filters for odor, and Floyd warns never to draw negative air from a crawlspace because of furnace backdraft [cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:29:36].

Floyd supplies the water-side sizing kit. Drying classes run Class 1 under 5% of surfaces wet, Class 2 at 5 to 40%, Class 3 over 40%, and Class 4 bound water. Refrigerant dehumidification is cubic feet divided by the class factor to get AHAM pints; desiccant is cubic feet times air changes per hour divided by 60 to get CFM. The 2015 air-mover rule is one per room, plus one per 50 to 70 square feet of floor, plus one per 100 to 150 square feet of wall and ceiling above 2 ft, plus one per offset over 18 inches, so a 750 square foot loss lands at 12 to 16 units, and water under 2 ft up the wall runs linear feet divided by 14 [cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:42:22]. TheIICRC's 2021 review stresses that those dehumidification formulas only give a minimum, and that Class 4 needs at least an LGR [bcid0F9jRTI @ 01:21:22]. Destry Ransdell at Restoration Technical Institute maps moisture with linear readings every 5 ft and floor readings every 5 by 5 ft, and marks equipment and migration lines on the sketch [XMpZ-8ZsSW8 @ 00:00:00]. The RTI Rover ride-on extractor moves about 1 square foot per 10 seconds: fantastic extraction, but “probably not the greatest” for large areas [XMpZ-8ZsSW8 @ 00:01:22].

Verification and hard measurement close the loop on every job. Nicole Bijlsma strongly recommends one air and one surface sample in every room suspected of elevated fungal particulates, calls spore count “the least important” number next to rank order, notes outdoor Aspergillus and Penicillium typically sit at only 5 to 10%, and flags a field tell: under the 2024 Condition 1, a spore-free air sample suggests a scrubber was running, which voids the test [r1JeD2hb2jM @ 00:14:00]. Coach8 insists the restorer use the same meter throughout a project, since Delmhorst, Tramex, Protimeter, Flir and Trotec readings differ by brand, and that readings be taken at least daily [7gZTdFWoHgs @ 00:37:15]. Floyd adds that an infrared camera “does not say it's wet or dry” and only shows a cooler surface, so always validate with the meter, and that non-penetrating meters cannot read through an air gap, while foil backing and metal throw false readings [cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:40:06]. On sequencing, the 2015 S520 rollout splits the roles: remediators may run post-remediation evaluation on their own jobs, IEPs perform post-remediation verification, a non-independent IEP must disclose that in writing, and PRV has to happen before any coating or sealant goes on [6CI2NAsooLw @ 00:12:57].

callout.title: Field Moves the Practitioners Swear By
callout.body: Small sequencing and paperwork habits that separate a defensible job file from a failed one.
items: Pull water off the top of the floor and from underneath before drying mats go down, otherwise you are sucking water through the mats; on the Rover, keep your weight forward and always run on slow [Restoration Technical Institute — XMpZ-8ZsSW8 @ 00:01:43]
Never draw negative air from a crawlspace: furnace backdraft is the risk Floyd flags right alongside the AFD filter stack [APPALeadership — cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:29:36]
Metric-edition owners of the 2021 S500 should strike the desiccant “divide by 60” line on page 176; Coach8 says that line needs to be lined out [Coach8 — 7gZTdFWoHgs @ 00:51:17]
On slabs, state in writing that you are unable to determine if the concrete is dried beyond the roughly 2 cm a scan meter reads [James Poon — r1JeD2hb2jM @ 00:41:14]

sop_steps.title: Stop the source and pick the standard
sop_steps.action: Get the water source stopped, then decide whether the loss is S500 drying work or S520 mold work.
sop_steps.detail: Melrose has a plumber stop the source first, works the 24 to roughly 72 hour S500 window, and switches to the S520 once mold exists [Andrew Melrose — iQ4PIKW3sEc @ 00:00:39]. Time's Dark Captains points to S500 8.6: when mold turns up on a water job, stop and contain [Time's Dark Captains — y00Yi4bnLx4 @ 00:20:45].

sop_steps.title: Seal and pressurize before anyone swings a hammer
sop_steps.action: Build 6 mil fire-retardant poly containment with critical barriers and establish -5 Pa before demolition.
sop_steps.detail: Never demolish or place air movers before sealing the room, then hold -5 Pa on a manometer [Balanced Building Biology — YdUmzaa5wO0 @ 00:02:30]. Floyd: decontaminate first rather than bringing in air movers that start blowing contamination around [APPALeadership — cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:23:50].

sop_steps.title: Physically remove, then clean to dust-free
sop_steps.action: Remove porous growth, HEPA vacuum, then damp wipe every surface.
sop_steps.detail: Drywall and insulation “got to go,” mold is pulled manually from concrete and wood, then a HEPA vacuum pass is followed by a microfiber damp wipe with dish soap and water to reach dust-free [Andrew Melrose — iQ4PIKW3sEc @ 00:06:03]. Stain removal stays the last cosmetic step, done only after the space is confirmed clean [Phill McGurk — Dl8DpDk97_A @ 00:04:11].

sop_steps.title: Dry, monitor, and verify before sealing
sop_steps.action: Take daily readings with one meter, then run post-remediation evaluation or third-party PRV before any coatings.
sop_steps.detail: Readings are taken at least daily, with the same meter used throughout the project [Coach8 — 7gZTdFWoHgs @ 00:35:55]. PRV happens before coatings or sealants, and a non-independent IEP must disclose that in writing [TheIICRC — 6CI2NAsooLw @ 00:12:57].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over who grades the job. Phill McGurk frames the IEP as the independent referee who performs post-remediation verification so the contractor never grades its own homework, and calls that independence the homeowner's ultimate quality control [Dl8DpDk97_A @ 00:05:15]. Jim Pearson, chairing the S520 consensus body, starts from field reality instead: most jobs have no IEP at all, so the 2024 edition forces the remediator to perform a post-remediation evaluation on every job, clean, dry and odor-free, and pushes IEP verification over to the S530 [JOiWfXdUwjM @ 00:23:10]. The Texas trainer behind Time's Dark Captains reads it tighter, arguing an IEP is needed to tell Condition 2 from Condition 1 and that remediators should not act as their own IEP under R520 page 93 [y00Yi4bnLx4 @ 00:37:12]. Nicole Bijlsma splits the difference by risk tier: the restorer or remediator evaluates recovery levels 0 to 1, while independent PRV covers levels 2 to 4, triggered by more than 10 square meters affected, occupant health concerns, or Category 2 or 3 water [r1JeD2hb2jM @ 00:30:41]. The operator playbook is to decide the recovery level at intake, because that single call determines whether your own sign-off closes the file or a third party has to.

Practitioners also fight over what counts as clean. Balanced Building Biology says the industry obsesses over total counts like under 1,000 spores, when rank order of species matters more, and indoor Aspergillus dominance is a problem even at lower totals [YdUmzaa5wO0 @ 00:01:44]. Bijlsma goes further, calling spore count the least important number and rank order far superior, and recommends one air and one surface sample in every suspect room [r1JeD2hb2jM @ 00:46:29]. Bijlsma anchors that comparison on the outdoor baseline, where Aspergillus and Penicillium typically make up only 5 to 10 percent of the count. Darren Floyd, with more than 30 years in the trade, offers the older playbook: there are no national thresholds, but some industrial hygienists use Penicillium and Aspergillus below about 3000 as a working line [cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:51:22]. Mark Cornelius pushes back from the commercial side, warning that cleaning to zero is pricing remediation out of the market because mold is so often uninsured, and telling the industry to stop trying to turn it into rocket science [jFMj8u8OsU4 @ 00:25:17]. The working split is clear: lab-driven operators sell species ranking, while count-driven shops anchor on a number the client and payer can follow, and both camps need the clearance yardstick agreed before the first sample is pulled.

On chemistry, the line between alternative playbook and violation runs through written disclosure. Andrew Melrose teaches a peroxide protocol they call the safest, paired with manually pulling mold from concrete and wood, while drywall and insulation simply have to go [iQ4PIKW3sEc @ 00:05:47]. Floyd gives the classic deviation case: mold was encapsulated instead of the drywall being removed because a computer and phone bank sat on the other side of the wall, and they insist a deviation is not a license to do something wrong but a detour to the same destination [cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:09:16]. The 2024 S520 panel now defines fog, mist and knockdown and permits knockdown of particulates, without loosening the remove-rather-than-kill rule [JOiWfXdUwjM @ 00:45:30]. The Texas trainer is the hard-liner, citing S520 section 5.8.1.1 that chemicals are not a substitute for removal and reading the standard to forbid scrubber mode without negative pressure [y00Yi4bnLx4 @ 00:32:28]. The split for an operator is practical, not philosophical. Melrose and Floyd show workable variations when a material or a site constraint forces it, while the Texas reading treats any chemical shortcut as indefensible. Whichever side you run, the variation has to be documented, communicated to affected parties, and authorized in writing before a single sprayer or encapsulant comes off the truck.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failures start with a job someone called dry. Melrose describes a house that had been dried that still had saturated materials and fresh mold, and warns that three or four days of fans proves nothing; only monitoring proves dryness [iQ4PIKW3sEc @ 00:02:41]. Balanced Building Biology names the concrete version the 2 cm trap: scanning meters miss moisture at the bottom of the slab, and the floor fails about three weeks later, which is why they call proper deep probing absolutely essential [YdUmzaa5wO0 @ 00:06:15]. Bijlsma turns that into a liability move, telling assessors to state in their disclaimer that they are unable to determine whether the concrete is dried beyond 2 cm, and notes Don was paid $5,000 for three hours of lectures on AS 2180/2170 sleeve testing [r1JeD2hb2jM @ 00:41:14]. Floyd adds the instrument traps: an infrared camera only says a surface is cooler and could be evaporation, so validate with a meter, and non-penetrating meters cannot read through an air gap while foil backing and metal throw false readings [cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:40:06]. Treat any reading you have not personally validated with a probe or a pin as unverified, and write the limitation into the file before the floor goes down.

The second cluster of failures is the crew spreading the problem it was hired to remove. Floyd warns that decontamination comes first, because rolling in a bunch of air movers before it just blows contamination around, and that a non-HEPA shop vac aerosolizes waterborne pathogens [cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:23:50]. Balanced Building Biology sets the sequence as a hard rule: never demolish or place air movers before the room is sealed with 6 mil fire-retardant poly, zip walls and critical barriers, and shop vacs and M-class extractors are not allowed [YdUmzaa5wO0 @ 00:02:30]. TheIICRC's S520 2015 briefing rejects misting disinfectants in lieu of source removal and warns that the rejected approach accomplishes a nice diffusion of the mold throughout the property, so it is not recommended at all [6CI2NAsooLw @ 00:12:38]. Bijlsma flags a quieter trap on the testing side: a spore-free air sample suggests a scrubber was running, which voids the test, so a too-perfect clearance result can sink the job rather than close it [r1JeD2hb2jM @ 00:12:14]. Every shortcut in this cluster converts a contained source into structure-wide fallout, so the operator rule is simple: seal, decontaminate, filter through true HEPA, and only then move air or pull clearance samples.

The money traps hit before and after the job. McGurk warns that general insurance almost always excludes mold and tells clients to demand a separate contractor's pollution liability policy, the mark of a true professional, and puts mold-specific insurance on their four-point hiring checklist [Dl8DpDk97_A @ 00:04:27]. Pearson adds that the standard is voluntary, but before a judge or jury a contractor who did not follow it is probably going to lose, and that deviation requires written full disclosure to the client; they relay Dave Dell's view that most firms lack adequate coverage [JOiWfXdUwjM @ 00:14:53]. The Texas trainer attacks the Harvey-era habit of whole-house flood cuts and says claiming compliance without doing the work is a shield made out of cardboard, adding that only the owner or owner's agent can impose limitations, never the adjuster working the claim [y00Yi4bnLx4 @ 00:27:34]. Cornelius supplies the backstory: the mold-is-gold era turned $2,000 water jobs into $40,000 mold jobs, and when bad actors surface the whole industry looks bad [jFMj8u8OsU4 @ 00:03:08]. Coverage, written deviation sign-off and an owner-signed limitations list are the three documents that decide whether a disputed job gets paid, gets reopened, or gets litigated in front of a jury.

callout.title: Four Stops Before Crew and Equipment Roll
callout.body: Clear these four practitioner-reported pitfalls before mobilizing on any S500 or S520 job.
items: Do not demolish or start air movers until containment is sealed and holding -5 Pa on a manometer [Balanced Building Biology — YdUmzaa5wO0 @ 00:02:47].
Do not close a drying file on fan-days; close it on monitored readings taken with the same meter used throughout the project [Coach8 — 7gZTdFWoHgs @ 00:37:15].

Do not deviate without documenting it, communicating with affected parties and getting written owner authorization; an adjuster cannot impose limitations [Time's Dark Captains — y00Yi4bnLx4 @ 00:12:13].
Do not take mold work without a separate contractor's pollution liability policy, since general insurance almost always excludes mold [Phill McGurk — Dl8DpDk97_A @ 00:04:27].

chapters.pull_quote: A deviation is not a license to do something wrong; it means there's another way to get there, kind of like a detour. Attributed to APPALeadership (cPAFOZbMKQE @ 00:09:16).
action_checklist: Stop the source and start mitigation as soon as safely possible after the water event [TheIICRC — bcid0F9jRTI @ 00:06:08].

Map moisture with linear readings every 5 feet and floor readings every 5x5 feet, marking equipment and any migration line on a full-size sketch [Restoration Technical Institute — XMpZ-8ZsSW8 @ 00:00:00].
Extract water off the top of and underneath the floor before drying mats go on, then run mats 10 seconds per position [Restoration Technical Institute — XMpZ-8ZsSW8 @ 00:01:43].
Once mold exists, switch to the S520 with 6 mil containment, negative air, high-CFM HEPA scrubbers, P100 respirators and decon chambers [Andrew Melrose — iQ4PIKW3sEc @ 00:03:54].
Pull one air and one surface sample in every suspect room and read rank order rather than raw spore counts [James Poon — r1JeD2hb2jM @ 00:14:00].
Save stain removal for last as a cosmetic step, done only after the space is confirmed clean [Phill McGurk — Dl8DpDk97_A @ 00:04:11].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I write and bill water mitigation estimates so cash-pay and insurance jobs get paid in full, and what mistakes lose money?
chapters.title: Water Mitigation Estimates and Getting Paid
chapters.subtitle: Cash-pay vs. insurance estimates, three ways to write mitigation, fighting adjuster reductions, Xactimate hacks and wet-drywall line items, the mitigation-to-rebuild tool and XactScope, mitigation/restoration cover sheets, a $50,000 lost-job lesson, and common mitigation errors
chapters.executive_summary: Shane O'Dazier, who reports more than a thousand water claims as an owner, runs a blunt playbook built on one premise: carriers 'control the end by controlling the means.' The answer is to write mitigation estimates heavy, before the work is done, as story-based 'muddy scopes' instead of line-item invoices. Albi of Restoration Success Strategies supports the core myth-busting: Xactimate and dry logs are not required to get paid in full. Shane moved mitigation to QuickBooks Online, and uses time-and-material sheets for jobs above roughly $18,000. The street numbers are $400-$500 per truck roll, a $2,000 cash-pay floor, a $285 initial response, $489 monitoring trips, half-day roundup billing worth $30,000-$40,000 a year, and a 10% streamline discount for immediate payment. Pushing back, ReconSmart insists documentation drives the estimate, never a target dollar figure. Jason Peters lost $50,000 after fronting a flood-insurance job.

key_metrics.label: Minimum Revenue Per Truck Roll
key_metrics.context: A sell/drop visit plus an equipment pickup puts a cash job near $800-$1,000 before any work, so a small cash pay is priced at $2,000.

key_metrics.label: Carrier Savings Per Water-Category Downgrade
key_metrics.context: Carriers argue cat 3 down to cat 2 and cat 2 down to cat 1 because each step cuts the bill. That is why Shane charges cat 3 pricing across the board.

key_metrics.label: Half-Day Roundup Equipment Billing
key_metrics.value: $30,000-$40,000 per year at 3-4 water jobs per week
key_metrics.context: Equipment days are billed as 3.4, 3.6 or 3.7 instead of a flat 3 on fans, dehumidifiers and scrubbers. Carriers pay it about half the time.

key_metrics.label: Per-Trip Monitoring Charge
key_metrics.context: An 'assess and reposition' return trip billed as a lump replaced roughly 3 hours at $50. It sat on a $7,300 invoice that was paid in full.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every speaker who touches billing agrees the money is won or lost on paper, not on the drying floor. Shane O'Dazier reports more than a thousand water claims as an owner. Shane frames the business as two problems: getting the job is the hardest thing in restoration, and getting paid is the second hardest [72Qh6dRR94U @ 00:13:38]. Shane reads carrier behavior as mechanical rather than moral. A publicly traded insurer carries a fiduciary duty not to overpay, which in practice becomes a duty to pay as little as possible. So an $8,000 bill that eventually settles at $6,000 'was never 8,000 to begin with' in the carrier's math [PqL0m54Gjb4 @ 00:04:07]. Carriers owe for damages, defined as cost incurred. That is why adjusters ask for an estimate and treat the word invoice 'like a curse word': an invoice implies finished, non-negotiable work [PqL0m54Gjb4 @ 00:06:05]. Shane's shorthand for the whole carrier strategy is that they 'control the end by controlling the means.' Albi of Restoration Success Strategies adds the leverage angle: insurers have not mastered first notice of loss. A flooded homeowner calls a plumber and a burning one calls 911, so restorers, not carriers, own the first contact on the job [kSobDHWEZJE @ 00:18:13]. The working conclusion across both camps is that the contractor who controls the paper controls the payout.

The second point of agreement is that Xactimate is a tool, not a prerequisite. Albi is an Xactimate certified trainer who has trained thousands of restorers on the platform, and still calls 'you have to use Xactimate' the biggest myth in the industry. Albi has coached dozens of contractors who built their own bills and were paid in full by both homeowners and insurance companies without it [kSobDHWEZJE @ 00:19:21]. Shane O'Dazier went further. Shane keeps Xactimate optional for reconstruction but pulled mitigation off it entirely, arguing that parent company Verisk assists in underwriting policies and earns most of its software revenue from adjusters [NyqgMvKRX14 @ 00:01:07]. Shane's sharpest specific charge is that Xactimate pricing has not risen with inflation year over year, while the same company serving insurers controls the price lists [SK7KHGnvQ6Y @ 00:04:59]. Operators who stay inside the software describe the same dynamic from the opposite direction. RestorationEze sells homeowners on its Xactimate estimates because the platform is likely the same system the adjuster uses to set reimbursement, so the number 'will be accepted' by the carrier [M1rrc7THcxU @ 00:01:00]. Neither camp claims the software itself is the villain. The fight is over who sets the numbers, and both sides treat the price list, not the drying science, as the battlefield.

The third point of agreement is that a mitigation estimate must carry risk and be written heavy up front. Shane O'Dazier's rule: if you are unsure whether drying takes four days or seven, write it for eight. The estimate is delivered before the work is done and should price the unknown. Shane writes stabilization as one to three days and drying as up to four days [PqL0m54Gjb4 @ 00:08:33]. The same logic drives Shane's remodel comparison: bid a bathroom at $21,000, finish it for $17,000, and the $4,000 gap is profit earned for absorbing risk, not a refund owed. Once the work is complete, Shane converts the estimate to an invoice without changing it [NyqgMvKRX14 @ 00:05:41]. Albi independently attacks the documentation crutch, calling dry logs a fad. Albi reports that Albi's own restoration company does not run them, that a Chicagoland competitor doing close to $100 million a year skips them as well, and that logs trending wetter still get paid [kSobDHWEZJE @ 00:15:05]. The guardrail both speakers repeat is consistency. Shane insists invoicing and billing must look the same job after job, a discipline the company lacked for years before fixing it [5CbcT0WZWts @ 00:08:15]. Inconsistent paper is what hands adjusters their ammunition.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Shane O'Dazier's first question on any job is who pays. Under about $5,000, the client may pay direct; a $15,000 water job almost always routes through insurance [72Qh6dRR94U @ 00:00:51]. For cash pays, the floor math is built on truck rolls. Every roll must make $400 to $500, so a sell-and-drop visit plus a pickup puts the job near $1,000 before any work. That is why a small cash pay lands at $2,000 [72Qh6dRR94U @ 00:02:07]. Price inside the thousand-dollar increments people actually pay in: $1,900 or $2,900, never $2,100. Past roughly $2,900 to $4,000, filing a claim usually makes more sense [72Qh6dRR94U @ 00:03:33]. The cash estimate itself can be three lines: initial response, work performed at the source of loss, and a return charge, because the client only cares about the bottom number. Jason Peters of On The Job hardened the self-pay side after a loss. Non-insurance customers now pay a deposit, and the job runs like construction, billed in thirds. Late fees run 5 percent at 30 days, 15 percent at 60 days and 20 percent at 90 days, with an attorney letter at 120 days [h3bbJRR6ceA @ 00:17:51]. Jason's rule now is that the company will not hold or front the bill any longer.

Inside the insurance estimate, the core weapon is what Shane O'Dazier calls the muddy scope. It is story-based and accurate, but built so adjusters reading from a flowchart lack the cost codes to attack. The first move is to lump services instead of pricing per unit. One line for work performed at the source of loss covered cabinets, countertops, tile, baseboard and drywall with a crew for two days; it was billed at $3,400 and paid [m97k7TBcJgY @ 00:06:33]. Strip sizes off dehumidifiers and charge for the most expensive unit, since a size on the line invites a 'did you need that size' fight. Charge cat 3 pricing on cat 1 work rather than let carriers save 30 to 40 percent by arguing the category down [NyqgMvKRX14 @ 00:08:48]. Rename what carriers refuse to pay for. An emergency service call during business hours becomes a 'service call' or an 'administration fee to relocate assets.' Equipment decontamination becomes a $289 lab restock fee entered as one unit [roHp-ZzbYvs @ 00:09:33]. Shane's own boundary is to change the pricing, not the scope. Chad Michael attacks the same leak from the adjuster's side. Carriers write 'R&R drywall' from the plain drywall category, when wet or contaminated drywall belongs under the water mitigation or hazardous materials categories, priced by water category [tYSY3Eo_nvA @ 00:01:44].

For shops still estimating in Xactimate, the mechanics are specific. Shane O'Dazier's half-day roundup bills dehumidifiers, air movers and scrubbers at 3.4, 3.6 or 3.7 days instead of a flat 3. Carriers pay it about half the time, which is worth $30,000 to $40,000 a year at three or four water jobs a week [roHp-ZzbYvs @ 00:07:49]. Some policies carry a mold cap of $2,000, $5,000 or $10,000. When they do, put insulation removal, disposal and access on the water mitigation estimate and keep only HEPA and mold-cleaning items on the mold estimate. Otherwise the carrier will burn $3,000 of a $5,000 allocation pulling crawl-space insulation [roHp-ZzbYvs @ 00:05:34]. Alfred of Xactimate Training by Crest LLC demonstrates the rebuild tool in the Professional version. Any mitigation estimate with at least two WTR items spawns a cloud copy with an R suffix. callout.title: Operator shortcuts that protect the bottom line
callout.body: Four field-tested moves for writing faster and defending numbers without arguing line by line.
items: Name saved estimates 'template_job type_amount_description' (for example, template water 7K two drying chamber). Typing 'template' then pulls every template, which ends the 10-15 minute code hunts and the forgotten air scrubbers. [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — roHp-ZzbYvs @ 00:01:23]

Bill the truck mount at $189 to $289 an hour for every hour the truck is committed, not just the hour spent extracting. That adds $300 to $400 per job. [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — roHp-ZzbYvs @ 00:10:41]

Stop negotiating line by line. Have the adjuster tally the attempted reductions and offer a 'streamline' discount capped at 10 percent in exchange for immediate payment. [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — roHp-ZzbYvs @ 00:11:38]
Use F9 notes to explain why each charge was used, its quantity and its duration, so an adjuster or reviewer reads the reasoning on the line itself. [ReconSmart Solutions LLC — 3DF6Xf4wlIg @ 00:08:38]

sop_steps.action: Decide insurance or direct-bill at first contact, and set deposit terms on self-pay jobs.
sop_steps.detail: Jobs under about $5,000 may go direct; $15,000 jobs go through insurance [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — 72Qh6dRR94U @ 00:00:51]. Self-pay jobs run on a deposit and thirds, with late fees on the contract [On The Job with Jason Peters — h3bbJRR6ceA @ 00:17:06].

sop_steps.title: Write the estimate heavy, before work completes
sop_steps.action: Price the uncertainty as ranges: stabilize 1-3 days, dry up to 4 days, crews up to 3 days.
sop_steps.detail: If unsure between 4 and 7 days, write 8, because the estimate carries the risk you absorb [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — PqL0m54Gjb4 @ 00:10:30].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over the estimating platform itself. Shane O'Dazier tells operators to get off Xactimate for mitigation, calling it the devil's tool because Verisk sells most of its seats to adjusters and assists in underwriting policies [NyqgMvKRX14 @ 00:01:07]. Shane says that while writing in Xactimate the team struggled to get a water job over $5,000, yet their QuickBooks muddy scope lands a $7,000 clean category one job [NyqgMvKRX14 @ 00:04:00]. RestorationEze runs the opposite playbook and sells Xactimate to homeowners as a trust signal: the estimator takes measurements, enters equipment and materials, and the software totals against accepted insurance reimbursement rates so the written estimate will be accepted by the carrier [M1rrc7THcxU @ 00:00:46]. Albi lands in the middle. As an Xactimate certified trainer who loves the product, Albi still calls the belief that you must use it the biggest myth in the industry, having coached dozens of restorers paid in full by homeowners and carriers without it [kSobDHWEZJE @ 00:19:08]. The practical fork is less about the tool than about whether your format hands the adjuster a line-item flowchart to attack or a story priced on your own rates.

Documentation is the second fault line. Shane calls over-documenting one of the biggest mistakes the company made for years, saying less is more because carriers ask for an estimate, not an invoice, and an estimate submitted before the work finishes cannot carry dry logs or completion photos [PqL0m54Gjb4 @ 00:00:54]. Albi backs the dry log skepticism from a different angle: their own company and a Chicago competitor doing close to a hundred million a year skip dry logs, and Albi has watched carriers pay on logs graphing the property getting wetter [kSobDHWEZJE @ 00:15:05]. ReconSmart takes the hard opposite line, teaching that physical loss conditions drive field activity, field activity drives documentation, and documentation drives the Xactimate estimate, never a target dollar figure worked backward [3DF6Xf4wlIg @ 00:07:53]. PuroClean treats documentation as the first step on site, capturing moisture readings, close-ups and 3D scans because every detail provides proof to the insurance company, and seeking carrier approval before demolishing cabinetry or flooring [HHLnyMyxcpQ @ 00:00:34]. Shane's compromise is timing: if an adjuster wants dry logs, hand them over once the carrier agrees to pay your price, not before.

Water category splits the room as well. Shane prices every job at category three rates and refuses to vary price by category, arguing carriers will always knock cat 3 to cat 2 and cat 2 to cat 1 because each step saves them 30 to 40 percent [NyqgMvKRX14 @ 00:09:03]. Chad Michael pushes the other way inside Xactimate: stop accepting adjuster R&R drywall from the plain drywall category and bill remove wet drywall and bag for disposal from the water mitigation or hazardous materials categories, priced at category three when water traveled through roofing, attic and insulation [tYSY3Eo_nvA @ 00:01:44]. Chad ties the right category directly to getting paid properly and to crews entering in proper protective equipment. On duration, Shane writes heavy and stays with it: unsure whether drying takes four or seven days, write eight [PqL0m54Gjb4 @ 00:08:33]. ReconSmart rejects that logic for equipment, warning that an LGR sitting in a photo does not automatically justify a five-day rental and that dehumidifier quantity and days must be supported by environmental conditions and project documentation [3DF6Xf4wlIg @ 00:05:11].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest firsthand failure comes from Jason Peters, who lost $50,000 on a two-week category three flood mitigation after the homeowners policy denied groundwater and only flood coverage remained [h3bbJRR6ceA @ 00:02:02]. The flood carrier refused mold items, cabinetry, multiple flooring layers, HEPA vacuuming and encapsulation, so Jason stripped those lines and dropped HMR codes to cat 3, a roughly $25,000 cut that left a $50,000 bill [h3bbJRR6ceA @ 00:11:19]. Months later Jason learned the insured had been cashed out on a $50,000 cap; the homeowner then hung up, refused the rebuild, and posted a Google review calling Jason a thief and a liar using mid-mitigation photos. Post-mitigation photos got the review removed and a lien was filed, but the money never came despite a signed work authorization and direct billing agreement. Jason's fix: self-pay jobs now run like construction with a deposit and thirds, plus late fees of 5 percent at 30 days, 15 percent at 60, 20 percent at 90 and an attorney letter at 120 [h3bbJRR6ceA @ 00:17:51]. Shane O'Dazier draws the same leverage lesson for reconstruction: do not start until both sides reach agreement, or you are screwing yourself [SK7KHGnvQ6Y @ 00:07:21].

Shane's recurring warning is that carriers either pay in full or cut the bill in half, and that half the files get reviewed while half do not [m97k7TBcJgY @ 00:07:17]. Accepting the cut redefines the loss: turn in $8,000, get cut to four, settle at six, and the damages were always $6,000, because carriers owe for cost incurred, not estimates [PqL0m54Gjb4 @ 00:04:07]. Detail is the attack surface. Equipment sizes invite arguments over whether a smaller dehumidifier would have done the job, so Shane drops sizes and charges the most expensive unit; hourly monitoring drew demands for time cards and cuts from 14 hours to three, so Shane bills a $489 assess-and-reposition trip [m97k7TBcJgY @ 00:05:03]. Overhead and profit labeled as such gets thrown out despite Xactimate's white paper saying you may charge it, so Shane builds margin into rates instead [NyqgMvKRX14 @ 00:09:43]. The mold cap trap is quieter: with a $5,000 mold allocation, the carrier can spend $3,000 of it pulling crawl space insulation and leave $2,000 for actual cleaning, so removal and disposal belong on the water estimate [roHp-ZzbYvs @ 00:05:34].

ReconSmart flags the field-to-file gaps that sink estimates: pulling equipment because another job needs it or a homeowner complained about fan noise is not proof the drying objective was achieved, which requires comparing affected materials against known dry reference readings [3DF6Xf4wlIg @ 00:07:10]. When eight air movers are billed but only six can be verified in photos and logs, ReconSmart says go back to the field team rather than invent a justification. Automation carries the same risk: Crest's Alfred warns the Xactimate rebuild tool must assume carpet grade and similar details, and those assumptions could be wrong unless reviewed [CFVMi9HmVcM @ 00:03:04]. On unit economics, Shane sets a floor of at least $400 to $500 every time a truck rolls, which is why small cash jobs requiring a return trip should land near $2,000 [72Qh6dRR94U @ 00:02:07]. Albi's margin math shows why the floor matters: about 33 percent direct job cost leaves roughly 67 percent gross profit, but customer acquisition and overhead squeeze mitigation-only shops to 20 to 25 percent EBITDA [kSobDHWEZJE @ 00:09:59].

callout.title: Clear These Four Gates Before You Start or Submit
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a loss, a cut, or a court threat the practitioners lived through. Run them on every water job before equipment leaves the truck or an estimate leaves the office.
items: No self-pay mitigation starts without a deposit, a thirds payment schedule, and contract late fees of 5 percent at 30 days escalating to an attorney letter at 120 days [On The Job with Jason Peters — h3bbJRR6ceA @ 00:17:06].

Lock one naming, bundling and pricing protocol and run it the same way on every claim; doing it sometimes makes you the hypocrite and destroys the pattern evidence that carriers paid it before [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — NyqgMvKRX14 @ 00:12:01].

Change your pricing, never your scope: do not write two days on site when the crew was there an hour, and do not write work you did not do [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — NyqgMvKRX14 @ 00:17:01].

Reconcile billed equipment against photos and equipment logs before submission; if eight air movers are billed and six are verified, investigate with the field team instead of inventing a justification [ReconSmart Solutions LLC — 3DF6Xf4wlIg @ 00:08:54].

chapters.pull_quote: "Getting the job is the hardest thing in restoration; getting paid is the second hardest." — Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits (72Qh6dRR94U @ 00:13:38).
action_checklist: Decide up front whether the job bills insurance or the client directly, and park cash-pay totals at the top of a thousand-dollar increment such as $1,900 or $2,900 [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — 72Qh6dRR94U @ 00:03:33].

Build named estimate templates holding every piece of equipment, so air scrubbers, negative air filters and injected drying never get left off the bill [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — roHp-ZzbYvs @ 00:00:57].
Bill fans, dehumidifiers and air scrubbers with half-day roundup increments such as 3.4 or 3.6 days instead of whole days [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — roHp-ZzbYvs @ 00:07:31].

When an adjuster tallies attempted reductions above 10 percent, offer a 10 percent streamline discount in exchange for immediate payment [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — roHp-ZzbYvs @ 00:11:38].
Create separate mitigation and restoration lines of coverage in the carrier profile so each prints its own cover sheet with taxes [Chris Hatcher — i4kOEeFrMaI @ 00:00:24].
Write contaminated drywall as remove wet drywall and bag for disposal from the water mitigation category instead of plain R&R drywall [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — tYSY3Eo_nvA @ 00:01:24].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I learn Xactimate and choose the right line items to build complete, accurate estimates?
chapters.title: Xactimate Fundamentals and Line-Item Mastery
chapters.subtitle: Xactimate 101 and claim information setup, line-item search and cheat sheets, wall and ceiling repair items, window tips, the May 2026 new line items, monthly price-list changes, global depreciation and bid items, mobile hacks, a full scoping walkthrough, code arguments with adjusters, and an estimate-writing chatbot
chapters.executive_summary: Xactimate is the working language of insurance restoration. Overhead And Profit puts carrier adoption above 80%, and Verisk reprices it every month. Practitioners agree on three things: the sketch drives quantities, Click-for-Detail hides money (an extra $225 on one window line), and commonly missed items belong on every file. Those items include detach-and-reset appliances, project management, anti-microbial and haul-off. The street mechanics are exact. Drying equipment bills per 24-hour unit-day. Dallas project management runs about $80 an hour commercial and $70 residential. A ceiling patch of 32 equals one 4x8 sheet. The May 2026 update lifted a one-zone mini-split from $1,500 to $4,200. The split between practitioners is posture. Chad Michael starts from the highest position and stacks code reasons. Carrier-side Canei Adjusting defaults to cheaper floor protection, standard insulation and one coat on white ceilings.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner here works from one premise. Xactimate is the shared currency between contractor, adjuster and carrier, and its prices move every month. Overhead And Profit states that more than 80% of carriers use Xactware, with prices set monthly by market [A7SLk2mjCXU @ 00:00:00]. Graham at Estimate Hub calls Xactimate the most widely used software in insurance and restoration. Graham confirms that Verisk pushes a new price list once a month, that material and labor swings flow through it, and that every jurisdiction carries its own tax [KeJzOY4eZHU @ 00:00:35]. The build order is just as settled. Estimate Mastery teaches it as a numbered run: claim info, sketch, items, photos as step 3.5, and the report last [Vj-mEgtLqUw @ 00:07:08]. Graham lists the same three parts that must exist before any final print: sketch, estimate items and photos. Graham also shows why the sketch comes first. Roof squares pass automatically from the drawing into the roof replacement line items, which Graham calls a really cool efficiency of the program [KeJzOY4eZHU @ 00:02:09]. The sketch is not decoration. It drives the quantities that every downstream line depends on. An operator who skips it ends up hand-feeding numbers the software would have computed on its own.

The second point of agreement is that money is lost on items nobody thought to write. Daughtry Construction Group's rule is that anything necessary on the job can be charged. They flag detach-and-reset on toilets, dishwashers, ovens, microwaves, refrigerators, stoves, washers and dryers as commonly overlooked [HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:02:37]. Estimate Mastery has worked with over 2,000 contractors across 12 years. They show a single window line where an extra $225 was left off because the estimator did not know what they did not know. The default single-hung vinyl item excludes low-E glass, and only Click-for-Detail reveals it [WNR0K0ubIoI @ 00:01:06]. Chad Michael pushes the same discipline from the contractor side. Chad lists items in the estimate even when an adjuster calls them included. Chad then uses the add item info note to paste Xactimate's own official description, which rebuts the claim that a component is already covered by waste or tear-off [Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:21:16]. Claim Daddy writes as a carrier-side adjuster, not a contractor, and still treats certain lines as non-negotiable. An anti-microbial line item and the water-category haul-off line go into every water file Claim Daddy writes [Qu-NqEwWWPk @ 01:18:58]. Both seats at the table agree that the default item is a starting point, not a finished line.

Overhead and profit is the third area where the speakers line up, at least on the number. Daughtry Construction Group sets the split at 10% overhead and 10% profit and ties it to jobs with three or more trades. They add that it is a fight on roofs and usually rejected on mitigation-only work. Even so, they would rather ask and be turned down than not ask at all [HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:06:18]. Estimate Mastery loads O&P at 10/10 in the estimate parameters. They back it with an opening statement quoting the O&P white paper, so the rationale sits on page one of the file [Vj-mEgtLqUw @ 00:10:07]. Canei Adjusting teaches from the adjuster seat rather than the contractor seat and lands on the same trigger: O&P requires coordination between trades, so the trade count on the file matters before the percentage does [Sk9blhK0GiU @ 00:13:19]. The same Canei session lays out the depreciation mechanic every operator has to explain to a homeowner. On a $10,000 item depreciated at 50%, the insured receives $5,000 up front and the other $5,000 on the back end [Sk9blhK0GiU @ 00:12:31]. Both sides of the table read the 10/10 line through the trade count first.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Speed starts with search. EstimateTV teaches working from the Search tab rather than Macros. Type a term like paint and press return, and Xactimate returns the first 100 matches. The results include options such as one coat or two coats, a (V) marks a variable item, and a double-click adds the item to the room [sSaHviAzZ6w @ 00:01:33]. The faster route is the selector code box. Type a category code and press space, and every item in that category lists out. For example, type INS for insulation, then narrow with bat or foil. The codes to memorize are PNT for paint, DRY for drywall, RFG for roof and STG for siding [sSaHviAzZ6w @ 00:02:17]. The Restoration Advisors Group built a personal cheat sheet at scale. They selected all their estimates, exported them to PDF and combined two years of work into a single 15,000-page file. They then exported it to TXT, because Excel is not worth the bother, and use Ctrl-F on a term like Oak to surface every related item ever written [qQzYZWLmaSI @ 00:00:12]. That text later trained a chatbot on their website, which the speaker says is not going to replace estimate writing. Once a set of items works, save it. Adjuster TV notes that X1 desktop macros sync to mobile, so a macro built at the desk travels into the field [dtHSqRxkHLA @ 00:03:54].

The unit economics are concrete. Daughtry Construction Group's rule for drying equipment is that 'these pay per 24 hour period per air mover and per dehumidifier.' Two air movers running three days is therefore a quantity of 6, and setup, teardown and daily monitoring hours are charged on top [HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:01:05]. Debris belongs on all work, roofs included. It is measured in tons, by pickup load or by 12, 20, 30 and 40-yard dumpster, at Dallas prices that Daughtry says vary by location and by month [HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:01:56]. Project management is the line most often missed. Their Dallas rates run about $80 an hour commercial and $70 residential, and final cleaning comes in near 29 cents a square foot commercial and 37 cents residential [HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:04:43]. Canei Adjusting supplies the drywall arithmetic from the carrier side. A patch quantity of 32 equals one 4x8 sheet. Joint tape runs 8 feet, or 4 feet if the ceiling stain touches the wall. The board specified is 5/8 drywall [BQZjEuyEaq4 @ 00:03:24]. Because Canei writes from the adjuster seat, those quantities show exactly what a carrier-side estimator expects to see on a ceiling patch.

Finishing mechanics separate a draft from a deliverable, and three practitioners walk through the exact clicks. Claim Daddy reprices after dropping in any macro. They set depreciation at 7.5 years on the second floor and 5 on the first and let automatic labor minimums apply. The sample water loss lands at roughly a $30,000 claim carrying about $6,000 in depreciation, a file they say would take about an hour working solo [Qu-NqEwWWPk @ 02:40:15]. Crest LLC shows the bulk version: Ctrl-A, Global Changes, Depreciation, uncheck do not change age, and enter 15 years. Labor-only items are skipped automatically [ZY8afiQROiI @ 00:00:35]. Crest also shows what happens when a contractor's real number replaces the line items. The worked example is a roofer at $8,600 excluding tax and O&P, then a bid of $8,200. The existing lines are zeroed through Taxes, O&P and Repaired. An RFG BID item is added as tax exempt with the note 'per Joe's roofing invoice', and an exclude note closes the loop [ZY8afiQROiI @ 00:11:10]. Estimate Mastery's closing routine is to resequence line numbers so they run clean, print the Final Draft report, and lay out photos at two images per page with annotations [Vj-mEgtLqUw @ 00:19:28].

callout.title: Line-Level Moves That Recover Money
callout.body: Small, repeatable moves that practitioners use to defend line items and catch price shifts before an adjuster does.
items: When an adjuster pushes back, Chad Michael opens every time, verbatim, with: 'which item or items in the estimate did you have a problem with.' [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:16:44]

Footnote both the removal and the replacement line. Chad Michael's 206-page estimate works as a 'database' the adjuster reviews item by item. [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:14:59]
On the new vanity detach item, which is priced well above plain removal, attach an F9 note justifying 'thoughtful extraction.' [Actionable — s4xCprLX1Yw @ 00:05:15]
Edit the macro after you drop it in. Graham changed roof waste from 10% to 15% and noted that O&P can be removed per line. [EstimateHub — PDF to ESX converter for Xactimate — KeJzOY4eZHU @ 00:02:27]

sop_steps.title: Load Claim Information
sop_steps.action: Enter the date of loss, inspection date, claim number, loss type and deductible before sketching.
sop_steps.detail: Confirm the policy was active by checking the date of loss against storm reports. Then enter the date inspected, the claim number, the wind loss type and the deductible. [Claims Adjuster of the Year — EDF71IxtN5w @ 00:00:44]

sop_steps.title: Sketch With Hotkeys
sop_steps.action: Draw rough room shapes first, then correct the measurements.
sop_steps.detail: Load the macro first. Use B for a square break, D for a door, M for a missing wall and W for a wall, then fix the dimensions once the shapes are down. [Claim Daddy — Qu-NqEwWWPk @ 00:38:05]

sop_steps.title: Write Items In Job Order
sop_steps.action: Sequence the items as remove, R&R accessories in the middle, then replace, and list items even if they are called included.
sop_steps.detail: Write the removal first, 'sandwich' the R&R accessories in the middle, then write the replacement. Ice and water goes first in Minnesota's climate zone. [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:11:47]

sop_steps.title: Reprice, Resequence, Print
sop_steps.action: Reprice against the current list, resequence line numbers, and print the Final Draft report.
sop_steps.detail: Resequence the line numbers, use the Final Draft report, and lay out photos at two images per page with annotations. [Estimate Mastery — Vj-mEgtLqUw @ 00:19:28]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is between the contractor who writes high and the field adjuster who writes lean. Chad Michael of The Practitioner says carriers are 'gonna try to push me down at all times,' so he opens 'from the highest position so that i can end up at the highest position' [Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:14:28]. To him, a 100% approval is a warning sign that means 'what did I miss,' not a win [Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:14:10]. Canei Adjusting builds the opposite default from the carrier chair. Swap the floor protection cloth for a cheaper option because insurers prefer it, write standard insulation, and let the contractor submit a receipt to collect the upgrade difference [Z7kbWUDeX6A @ 00:02:43]. On ceilings, the same adjuster names plastic film as 'what most insurance companies will go for' and notes that contractors reach for costlier protection [BQZjEuyEaq4 @ 00:01:40]. Daughtry Construction Group lands closer to Chad. Anything necessary on the job can be charged, and on O&P for mitigation-only jobs, 'I'd rather ask and be turned down than to not ask at all' [HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:06:37]. The operator read is that carriers anchor low by default. A contractor estimate that mirrors the adjuster macro gives up the negotiation before the first email goes out, and it leaves nothing to trade back when the reviewer starts cutting.

Paint coats and O&P show the same rift line by line. Daughtry Construction Group writes 2 coats on new items and 1 coat on existing painted items being matched, and always charges mask and prep as separate lines [HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:04:07]. Canei Adjusting reports that carriers allow 1 coat for white ceilings and 2 for dark, while public adjusters and contractors push for 2 coats across the board [BQZjEuyEaq4 @ 00:10:29]. On O&P, Daughtry sets 10% overhead and 10% profit when three or more trades are involved. Daughtry calls it a fight on roofs and admits it is usually rejected on mitigation-only work [HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:06:18]. Estimate Mastery hard-codes O&P at 10/10 in the estimate parameters and loads an opening statement quoting the O&P white paper, so the justification rides on page one before any adjuster reads a line item [Vj-mEgtLqUw @ 00:10:56]. Canei Adjusting's claim-information walkthrough treats O&P as earned only when the job requires trade coordination [Sk9blhK0GiU @ 00:13:19]. In practice, Daughtry and Estimate Mastery put the argument inside the estimate itself, while the adjuster side waits to see whether coordination exists before releasing the 20%. Arm the file before the adjuster asks, because the roof and mitigation-only fights Daughtry describes are the default, not the exception.

The practitioners also split on how to move an adjuster. Chad Michael first tries to educate gently, even showing codes on a phone. If that fails, he pushes as far as possible, accepts the payment, and then goes back again [Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:01:18]. He opens every pushback email with the same line: 'which item or items in the estimate did you have a problem with' [Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:16:44]. He adds that a re-inspect starts things over, so you are 'not bound' by the first number [Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:04:38]. Claim Daddy warns from inside the carrier workflow that reviewers 'don't want you kind of trying to think you're educated or smart,' so you will have a much easier time just replacing drywall [Qu-NqEwWWPk @ 00:18:55]. On countertops, Daughtry Construction Group writes detach-and-reset first because insurers want it, then supplements for replacement if the top breaks [HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:03:15]. Claim Daddy counters that a contractor landing $5k over a $32k estimate in a 30-40k fee tier means no T&E for the adjuster, and that writing it right the first time is the fix. Graham of EstimateHub describes the middle path. When the contractor is 'a little bit more,' the parties reconcile by email or phone, and 'sometimes it does take a long time' [KeJzOY4eZHU @ 00:04:57].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap the practitioners measured is trusting the price list to keep pace with the market. Overhead And Profit reports that in North Texas in April 2016, suppliers raised prices about 5%, yet the May update moved only about $30 on a $20k estimate [A7SLk2mjCXU @ 00:02:10]. After the NTRCA email campaign, prices climbed in June, July, and August, and repricing a single estimate added $2,688.91 [A7SLk2mjCXU @ 00:03:14]. Actionable shows the reverse shock in May 2026. A one-zone mini-split jumped from $1,500 in April to $4,200, and a four-zone unit went from $6,800 to $13,000 after the labor yield dropped about 85% [s4xCprLX1Yw @ 00:18:33]. Their verdict: 'if you were trying to do mini splits in April, you were not making money.' The same update raised the steep-roof yield from 2.084 to 2.193, about 5%, and a higher yield means a lower price on every square [s4xCprLX1Yw @ 00:17:36]. Graham of EstimateHub confirms that Verisk updates the lists once a month, with materials and labor fluctuations flowing through and each jurisdiction carrying its own tax [KeJzOY4eZHU @ 00:00:35]. Claim Daddy closes the loop on the desk side by repricing after every macro is loaded [Qu-NqEwWWPk @ 02:40:15].

The second failure mode is money left on the table through line items nobody opened. Estimate Mastery says that after working with over 2,000 contractors across 12 years, most make the same mistake. On one window estimate, 'it's an extra $225 that's been left off' because the estimator did not know a single line item [WNR0K0ubIoI @ 00:01:06]. The fix is reading Click-for-Detail on single-hung vinyl windows, where low-E glass is excluded, and adding retrofit add-on items for the harder install [WNR0K0ubIoI @ 00:00:27]. Daughtry Construction Group lists the usual leaks. Detach-and-reset on toilets, dishwashers, ovens, microwaves, refrigerators, stoves, washers, and dryers is 'commonly overlooked' [HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:02:37]. Project management, at about $80/hr commercial and $70/hr residential in Dallas, is often missed. Chad Michael counters the 'included with waste/tear-off' denial by using add item info note to paste the official Xactimate description straight into the estimate [Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:21:16]. His Liberty Mutual job shows the size of the gap. The adjuster sat at $27,000 against his $400,000, and '300 and something' was added back later after that adjuster read the estimate [Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:22:29]. Every missed line is pure margin handed back to the carrier.

The third cluster is scope that gets rejected or capped no matter how it is written. Claim Daddy rejected a contractor's demand to remove all second-level exterior walls because the moisture meter did not support it. The contractor later admitted of the stair claim, 'i don't really know if it was really related' [Qu-NqEwWWPk @ 01:53:04]. The same adjuster flags regrout or recolor for plaster debris as 'probably going to get rejected' [Qu-NqEwWWPk @ 02:04:10] and warns that replacing every cabinet 'is an easy rejection by most insurance companies.' Canei Adjusting reports that tree debris is capped at $500 roughly 90-95% of the time, and sometimes at $1,000 [Sk9blhK0GiU @ 00:09:51]. Actionable relays a Shelter denial of utilities on a Cleveland, Ohio rental written on a DP-6. That denial is why you collect 3 months of utility bills before using the new electricity-consumption bid item [s4xCprLX1Yw @ 00:08:26]. The human bottleneck is memory. Claim Daddy tells estimators to 'never go off strictly off your memory' and to always review the photos [Qu-NqEwWWPk @ 01:17:58]. He labeled all 109 photos with a default caption first and hit renumber every time, because one extra claim per day is huge.

callout.title: Four checks before any estimate leaves the desk
callout.body: Each gate comes from a loss, rejection, or bottleneck a practitioner hit firsthand. Clear all four before you print the Final Draft report.
items: Reprice after every macro load and after each monthly price list update before sending the estimate [Claim Daddy — Qu-NqEwWWPk @ 02:40:15].
Open Click-for-Detail on window and newly added line items to catch exclusions like low-E glass before pricing [Estimate Mastery — WNR0K0ubIoI @ 00:00:27].
On far-apart new damage, send the photo report first and expect a re-inspect before building the full estimate [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:03:03].
Collect 3 months of utility bills before writing the electricity-consumption bid item, because Shelter denied utilities on a DP-6 rental [Actionable — s4xCprLX1Yw @ 00:08:26].

chapters.pull_quote: "They're gonna try to push me down at all times but I need to start from the highest position so that I can end up at the highest position." — Chad Michael - The Practitioner (Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:14:28).
action_checklist: Find items through the Search tab, not Macros: type a category code like INS in the selector box and press space to list every item in that category [EstimateTV — sSaHviAzZ6w @ 00:02:17].

Write the estimate in job order: remove, then R&R accessories in the middle, then replace. List items even if 'included' and footnote both removal and replacement lines [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — Lh586v6HcYw @ 00:11:47].
Label photos before sketching: set a default caption on every photo first, refine it, and always hit renumber [Claim Daddy — Qu-NqEwWWPk @ 00:24:05].
Bill air movers and dehumidifiers per 24-hour period per unit (2 movers for 3 days = 6), plus setup, teardown, and daily monitoring hours [Daughtry Construction Group — HLwvN9mF1R0 @ 00:01:24].
For a contractor bid, zero the lines via Taxes/O&P/Repaired, then add a tax-exempt RFG BID item noted 'per Joe's roofing invoice' [Xactimate Training by Crest LLC — ZY8afiQROiI @ 00:11:10].
Export all past estimates to TXT, not Excel, and Ctrl-F the combined file to find related line items fast [The Restoration Advisors Group — qQzYZWLmaSI @ 00:01:15].

chapters.question_prompt: How do roofing contractors supplement insurance claims to recover items the adjuster's estimate missed?
chapters.title: Roof Claim Supplementing
chapters.subtitle: Proving estimates wrong line by line, the 12 roof components that matter in Xactimate, Texas supplement writing, who to send the supplement to, explaining supplements to homeowners, maxing roof-only claims, in-house vs. outsourced supplementers, 15-minute roof and siding estimates, and measurement-to-contract workflows
chapters.executive_summary: Roofing supplement practitioners agree the first carrier estimate is short and must be rebuilt line by line against evidence: measurement reports, tear-off photos, code citations, and bolded notes on every changed line. Estimate Mastery took a $21,027 RCV file to $47,192 with O&P. Roof Sales Mastery pegs the real average supplement at $4,000 to $4,500 and sells a 100-plus item master list, macros, and homeowner letters it says win O&P 75 to 80% of the time. Chad Michael submits before the build and over the field adjuster's head, concedes small items for rapport, and reports 40%-plus increases. Dustin Taylor writes full redecks from attic photos to stay in the conversation. American Roof Supplements pushes back on maximization, aiming for the most accurate, supportable estimate and charging $50 per estimate and $150 per supplement.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner on the roofing side starts from the same premise: the first carrier estimate is short, and the gap is systematic rather than accidental. Becca Switzer of Roof Sales Mastery frames it as carrier math, a State Farm saving of $1,000 on each of 500,000 claims, and tells contractors to supplement 100% of claims because a file never comes back with everything paid [jj-GWZEtOc0 @ 00:02:33]. The same channel's sales call runs the math at 100,000 claims times $1,000 for $100M, while the contractor-side version is 100 claims times $10,000 for $1M [q63afBPc6eY @ 00:02:12]. Adjusters are described as paid to mitigate loss, with one Liberty Mutual adjuster's card literally reading "loss mitigation," so objections are expected as part of the job rather than taken personally [sICOGLUjsao @ 00:13:18]. Chad Michael adds the operational layer: start the dumpster, wet drywall removal, materials, and permits to "plant our flag" and keep the claim moving instead of waiting on the carrier [4dhIe6HGIs0 @ 00:16:20]. Even the most accuracy-focused shop, American Roof Supplements, opens its sample file with a carrier estimate of about $12,000 carrying "10 smaller things" wrong, not one dramatic miss, which is exactly the kind of leakage the volume-driven channels build their entire pitch around [HpoMhPz1KfU @ 00:00:52].

The second point of agreement is that a supplement is built line by line against the carrier's own estimate, with evidence attached to every difference. American Roof Supplements lays the two estimates side by side, lists existing quantity, proposed quantity, and evidence for each line, labels photos by roof location, strips out unsupported upgrades, then runs a "Show me why" test on the whole file [HpoMhPz1KfU @ 00:08:20]. Its beginner workflow runs seven steps: get the carrier estimate, gather evidence, compare line by line, identify legitimate differences, build or revise with notes, organize documentation, and submit and respond [TkCEjbO6vQs @ 00:04:30]. Chad Michael works the same direction, reconciling from the top of the carrier estimate downward, backed by a PDF of codes and photos [4dhIe6HGIs0 @ 00:02:16]. American Roof Supplements reduces every roof component to four questions, namely what it is, where it is, how it is measured, and what documents it, and uses that drill to keep eave footage separate from rake footage, count pipe boots that aerials hide behind dormers, and avoid confusing the ridge cap with the vent underneath it [DR03Zlogfe0 @ 00:00:48]. The shared rule under all four voices is blunt: measurements drive quantity changes, photos drive damage items, cited requirements drive code items, and anything discovered at tear-off gets photographed before it is covered back up.

Practitioners also agree on how the file should look and how hard to push. Estimate Mastery bolds every changed line and adds a note explaining why its line items differ from the original statement of loss, so the reviewer sees the argument without hunting for it [q6R8Iom5Uz8 @ 00:13:44]. Nobody recommends trench warfare over small items. Chad Michael concedes roughly $100 items on purpose to build rapport and keeps phone calls with adjusters friendly rather than combative [bVX2IRINNSM @ 00:28:20]. Becca Switzer is "not teaching you guys to argue for fifteen days over a turtle vent" and calls $5,800 received against a $6,700 ask good enough to close [jj-GWZEtOc0 @ 00:18:01]. The homeowner has to be briefed before any of this starts. Adam Bensman of The STRONG Roofer explains the supplement at color selection at the latest, reframes price as an objective assessment, walks through Xactimate as the third-party platform insurers use, and pitches the evidence packet as protection from surprise costs that "doesn't change a darn thing for you" [zxGa72oAf0w @ 00:02:17]. The warning attached is sharp: homeowners left without a narrative invent one, decide the contractor is a "slime ball" chasing free money, and the job ends with uncollected money and bad reviews instead of referrals.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The build itself runs on macros. Alina Wilson of Estimate Mastery keeps over 120 macros and says they are the only way to write a full roof and siding estimate in 10 to 15 minutes, because the search bar is slow and extra characters pull up the wrong item [fdW0W_-MR-s @ 00:01:00]. The rules are specific: one trade per macro, double-click to load it into the item or quick-entry screen, fill calculator fields from the roof report including waste, and treat the loaded macro as a checklist, deleting lines like a gable cornice return only after checking photos, field notes, and the measurement report. Wilson used to leave off chimney flashing while running a third-party supplementing business until it went on the macro. Roof Sales Mastery puts a hand-built estimate at 30 to 35 minutes and says macros cut that in half [sICOGLUjsao @ 00:00:39]. Dustin Taylor structures the Texas file with bold F9 headings for carrier approved line items and supplement line items, mirrors the carrier's order, and runs a macro drop with "skip duplicates" turned on, which caught 2 items on that job [gtsj3GY7D8c @ 00:20:19]. Chad Michael orders the estimate as a sandwich that follows the job: removes first, then accessory R&R, then replaces [bVX2IRINNSM @ 00:26:28].

The money lives in specific line items. Estimate Mastery's sample file started at $21,027 RCV on a May 2024 price list, was repriced to April 2025 on the argument that nobody can buy gas at 2024 prices, switched three-tab to architectural, added starter on rakes and hips at a unit price of 8.57, then layered fascia, vents, rain caps, code-cited ice-and-water, hand-load labor, tarp and contents labor, project management hours, and permit to reach $47,192 RCV with O&P [q6R8Iom5Uz8 @ 00:19:04]. Dustin Taylor corrected a carrier bid of 29-gauge metal to the 22 gauge actually on the roof, roughly 5.40 versus 9 per LF, about $4 per LF more, and used the 24-gauge line because no 22-gauge item exists in Xactimate [gtsj3GY7D8c @ 00:03:20]. Becca Switzer's fascia substitution swaps roughly $3 per foot prefab for $10 per foot custom-bent, turning $400 into $1,200, and the master list math says asking for 18 items and getting half approved yields 9, triple the old result [jj-GWZEtOc0 @ 00:10:15]. Chad Michael caught a missing ridge cap of about 240 to 250 LF and argued waste should be 15% rather than the adjuster's 10% once ridge, starter, and valley are counted inside it [bVX2IRINNSM @ 00:03:52].

Routing and packaging are treated as mechanics, not afterthoughts. Chad Michael never sends the supplement to the field adjuster, because that invites them back out and prolongs the claim, and instead submits over everybody's head to ASI corporate claims, before the build, within 2 days, setting a 2-week expectation so a one-week answer looks like over-delivery [bVX2IRINNSM @ 00:19:04]. At State Farm, the move is getting past the robot and asking for Team 53, whose inside adjusters carry more authority than the field adjuster. Becca Switzer packages everything into one PDF rather than 62 attachments, opens with a non-aggressive "as you requested" paragraph, and gives each item its why, documentation, and a photo, adding an O&P cover sheet [jj-GWZEtOc0 @ 00:20:34]. Objection handling runs on "if this then that" scripts with 2 to 5 rounds expected, such as asking $5k and settling at $4k, while roughly 1 in 20 adjusters simply approve [sICOGLUjsao @ 00:14:46]. Homeowner letters are the escalation "dynamite": the sales call claims O&P lands 75 to 80% of the time once the letter goes in, drawn from 25 to 30 templates covering partial approvals, discontinued materials, stonewalling, preferred contractors, and multiple bids [q63afBPc6eY @ 00:07:50].

callout.title: Small Moves That Move the Check
callout.body: Line-level leverage points practitioners use to unlock O&P, beat component objections, and set the negotiating anchor.
items: One interior water spot unlocks O&P on the whole job; Chad Michael cites a $28,000 job with a $5,400 to $5,600 gap riding on a single closet water spot [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — bVX2IRINNSM @ 00:43:18].
When State Farm says masking is included in paint, pull the Xactimate component breakdown and show it lists no masking materials [Roof Sales Mastery — Jvj3So17gtA @ 00:01:55].

Start A-bucket items from the highest position, such as detach-and-reset instead of mask; on a Florida file where $8K was cut to $4K, the play was sending $16K [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — 4dhIe6HGIs0 @ 00:09:28].
Use the State Farm summary sample page showing GC O&P at 10 and 10 as leverage in the homeowner conversation [Estimate Mastery — q6R8Iom5Uz8 @ 00:02:00].
