sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is philosophy. American Roof Supplements sets the goal as 'the most accurate, supportable estimate for the legitimate covered work,' rejects aiming for the biggest possible estimate, and warns that 'habits are not line items': anything added out of routine rather than because the roof shows it has no place on the file [TkCEjbO6vQs @ 00:04:15] [HpoMhPz1KfU @ 00:10:06]. Roof Sales Mastery runs the opposite play. Ridge, starter, O&P and drip edge are the 'basic BS' every adjuster has a scripted rebuttal for, so the money lives in a master list of 100-plus items: cornice returns, generators, harnesses, OSHA supervision hours, ladder jacks, a single-axle dump truck, hand loading, window cleaning. They wave off the 'fluffing' charge because the adjuster decides what gets paid [q63afBPc6eY @ 00:04:41]. Chad Michael sits closer to Roof Sales Mastery on the opening position: start every item from the highest position, detach-and-reset instead of mask, and when a Florida carrier cut $8K to $4K, the counter went out at $16K [4dhIe6HGIs0 @ 00:09:28]. The operator choice is whether the file reads as an audit trail of one specific roof or as an opening anchor built off a master checklist, and the two camps price their services and train their people around those opposite answers.

Routing and posture split next. Chad Michael never sends the supplement to the field adjuster, because that invites them back out and prolongs the claim. The file goes 'over everybody's head' to corporate claims, and it goes in before the build, so the contractor learns which items the carrier will resist while there is still time to photograph them. That is the 'two bites at the apple' play, with a target of submission within two days and a response inside a week [bVX2IRINNSM @ 00:00:30] [bVX2IRINNSM @ 00:18:44]. Roof Sales Mastery's Becca Switzer is softer on tone and longer on persistence: open with a non-aggressive 'as you requested' paragraph, attach the why, the documentation and a photo to every line, work if-this-then-that objection scripts, and take the compromise, because $6,700 asked against $5,800 received is good enough [jj-GWZEtOc0 @ 00:18:01]. Estimate Mastery adds a third posture: play strictly by Xactimate's inclusion rules whether they help or hurt, which is why pipe jack and exhaust cap removal stay folded into shingle removal while RNR drip edge earns its own line [q6R8Iom5Uz8 @ 00:04:08]. The tension is speed versus rapport: going over heads compresses the timeline, while the conciliatory email keeps the adjuster in the deal across two to five rounds.

O&P and decking are where the playbooks diverge on proof. Roof Sales Mastery calls the three-trade requirement a 'smoke screen objection' and builds an entire module around maxing out roof-only claims on brick homes that carry nothing but three-tab shingles and felt, with no gutters to add [Jvj3So17gtA @ 00:00:35]. Chad Michael counters with history: the three-trade rule shifted around 2011 to 'complexity and/or coordination,' started by State Farm, and there is no law behind it, so the fight is over logged coordination rather than trade count [4dhIe6HGIs0 @ 00:24:47]. On decking, Dustin Taylor wrote a full redeck on a Texas file off attic photos, with no tape-measure proof of the spaced-deck gap, explicitly 'to be in the conversation' with the carrier [gtsj3GY7D8c @ 00:18:16]. American Roof Supplements draws the hard line against that move: do not assume decking damage, capture a wide photo, a close photo, measurements and location, and remember that 'necessary replacement does not automatically mean covered replacement' [HpoMhPz1KfU @ 00:06:18]. Operators running the Taylor play are betting the carrier negotiates off whatever scope is written down; operators running the American Roof Supplements play are betting that a clean evidence chain wins the line on the first pass without a second round of argument.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most repeated failure is documenting too late or trusting the aerial. American Roof Supplements names five core mistakes: supplementing from memory, adding items without evidence, assuming every roof uses the same items, assuming Xactimate pricing settles every cost dispute, and documenting too late. Tear-off discoveries get photographed before they are covered, or they are gone [TkCEjbO6vQs @ 00:08:30]. The same shop warns that aerial images cannot see wall flashing, that pipe boots hide behind dormers on measurement reports so the count has to come off the actual roof, and that valleys must never be guessed from satellite [HpoMhPz1KfU @ 00:05:03] [DR03Zlogfe0 @ 00:06:47]. Estimate Mastery's Alina Wilson, who previously owned a third-party supplementing business, admits to constantly leaving off chimney flashing until it went onto a macro that forces a decision every time: deal with the line or delete it [fdW0W_-MR-s @ 00:03:48]. Wilson also flags the Xactimate search bar as a trap in its own right, because it is slow and a few extra characters pull up the wrong line item. The fix the three converge on is a checklist loaded before the estimate is written, then checked against photos, field notes and the measurement report, rather than memory applied after the fact.

The second failure mode sits on the homeowner side. Adam Bensman of The STRONG Roofer says that when the supplement is explained badly, homeowners assume the contractor is chasing their insurer for 'free money,' worry about the deductible, and the contractor ends up 'not collecting money and bad reviews.' Without a narrative for what happens next, homeowners invent one and cast the roofer as a 'slime ball' [zxGa72oAf0w @ 00:01:05] [zxGa72oAf0w @ 00:08:27]. Bensman's fix is timing, explaining it at color selection or the deposit check at the latest, and framing it as protection from financial surprises. American Roof Supplements adds the mirror trap: never promise the homeowner payment, because construction scope and insurance coverage are different questions [HpoMhPz1KfU @ 00:07:44]. Inside the company, the same channel reports owners who tell their sales force 'supplements don't work,' pay reps commission on the original amount, and collect the supplement money themselves on the back end; their fishing analogy says the best bait is the one you believe in [wi2YpyR1was @ 00:03:00]. Roof Sales Mastery's counterpart warning: when reps supplement their own jobs, results go inconsistent, rep number two pulls about half of rep number one, and a lazy rep simply lets items go.

The economics checks cut against the marketing. Chad Michael warns that 10 and 10 O&P is not your margin, puts the target at 50 to 70 percent profit, and refuses to spend an hour arguing over 10 feet of drip edge [4dhIe6HGIs0 @ 00:42:38]. Roof Sales Mastery's own figures need auditing before anyone builds a forecast on them. One sales call advertises a $4,500 average across 165 jobs for $742,500, cites Brad at $45,400 across five supplements while speaking the average as '$980,' and then resets the realistic expectation at $6,000 to $7,000 [q63afBPc6eY @ 00:10:27]. On a separate call the same channel advertises a $2,500 average, calls the 'real' figure $4,000 to $4,500, and runs the floor case: 100 claims at just $250 each is still $25,000 [sICOGLUjsao @ 00:20:09]. Becca Switzer's carrier-level reality check is blunter: Allstate and Safeco may pay 2 of 11 items, and the stated expectation is a $2,500-plus average increase per claim [jj-GWZEtOc0 @ 00:18:50]. Time is the other cost line. Estimate Mastery will not chase about $100 in repricing, and Roof Sales Mastery says untrained supplementing takes three times as long, which is the per-hour test behind the drip-edge rule.

chapters.question_prompt: How should contractors deal with insurance adjusters and public adjusters, and what are the legal limits on contractor advocacy?
chapters.title: Adjusters, Public Adjusters, and the Negotiation Table
chapters.subtitle: Negotiating mitigation invoices, breaking contractor-adjuster stalemates, questioning adjuster demands, reading carrier estimates, what public adjusters do, roofer vs. PA conflicts, PA vs. insurance lawyer, the seven levels of PA claims, a denied-claim reversal, and UPPA and contingency-contract risks
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners across public adjusting, roofing, and restoration agree that the carrier's first Xactimate number is a weak baseline to be attacked, not accepted: Frontline paid about $40,000 against an almost $75,000 bid, and Chad Michael never settles. Contractors may discuss scope and pricing but not negotiate coverage, with Texas UPPA rules voiding power-of-attorney workarounds. Street mechanics include reading squares and tear-off quantities, catching unit errors like 24.48 SF entered for 2,448 SF, switching DMO removal codes to trade codes for roughly 40 percent approval, running a recorded adjuster recap, and Shane O'Dazier's 3-to-4-minute question-list close with a 10 percent discount ceiling. Disagreements run deep: Vince Perri says PAs win more money 10 times out of 10, FirehouseEducation tells restorers never to deal with PAs, and an insurer-side lawyer argues a 10 percent fee leaves owners unable to fully repair.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who has sat across from a carrier agrees on the opening truth: the insurer's first number is a starting position it wrote for itself, not a verdict. claimhelpme calls it the baseline problem, warning that “A weak estimate creates a weak starting point” and that when the low figure goes unchallenged, every later conversation negotiates down from it rather than up from the real scope [2WVlG5yPBTU @ 00:03:46]. Builder's Perspective Public Adjusting puts dollars on the gap, walking through a file where Frontline paid about $40,000 against a contractor bid of almost $75,000 on a scope he describes as relatively similar, which is why he tells owners to wait for the carrier's paperwork before deciding whether to bring in a PA [kWxJ6PIkM-M @ 00:00:33]. Chad Michael takes the hardest line: “you should never agree to settle ever with an insurance company ever no matter where you are in the process,” even when the adjuster climbs from $20K to about $30K against a $40K contractor number, because an estimate is only “a prediction of the future” and the contractor holds the power [vkrXTVQcVQQ @ 00:00:59]. On Roofing Insights, a State Farm direct payment of $5,000 became $17,000 once a stormchaser worked the same claim [uykTx34p0Js @ 00:11:02].

The second point of agreement is where the legal lines sit, and contractors who blur them get burned. Vince Perri, citing Florida statute, says a contractor may suggest filing a claim and may discuss its bid for usual and customary fees, but may not negotiate the claim, which is the PA's lane [RRn3mzn9xCw @ 00:09:43]. Builder's Perspective Public Adjusting draws the same boundary from the other side: a contractor cannot act as the PA on the same claim, though it can still talk through its own pricing with the carrier [kWxJ6PIkM-M @ 00:01:10]. John Black of Daly & Black lists the Texas functions that trigger unauthorized practice of public adjusting, including investigating, appraising, evaluating or advocating, preparing or negotiating the claim, advising on policy terms, and advertising as an adjuster, and he shuts down the permission or power-of-attorney workaround under Texas Insurance Code section 4102.163, leaving a contractor with a void contract and a policyholder who can refuse to pay [jaGktNyKvE4 @ 00:01:55]. Dimmitri Lipinski reduces it to one rule on Roofing Insights: roofers may discuss scope only, not coverage, interior damage, or hotel costs, and anything past that line is UPPA exposure [uykTx34p0Js @ 00:20:28].

The third consensus point is that the file wins, not the volume of the argument. Chad Michael's standard is a photo, a code citation, and a footnote for every line item, built with Xactimate's item image and add item info note functions so the adjuster sees exactly what each code includes [vkrXTVQcVQQ @ 00:06:44]. Chris Zimmerman tells contractors to walk into the first meeting carrying the estimate, homeowner-facing evidence, damage photos, technical bulletins, building codes, and a detailed scope, because “If you want to be taken seriously, you need to be someone who deserves to be taken seriously” [LwNOcenSP_c @ 00:01:13]. American Roof Supplements adds the photo discipline: shoot the overall slope before the detail, include a measurement, label everything, and remember that “The contractor's job is to make the technical facts clear, not to promise what the policy will pay” [zDKvQs0viSI @ 00:02:50]. Daniel Kern of The Adjuster's Roundtable shows where that discipline leads on a hard file: a Hurricane Helene loss on two buildings, denied as flood on one and pre-existing damage on the other, was taken to policy limits after he brought in vetted experts, prepared rebuild estimates, and presented a full documentation package [_wmRAji2ZmI @ 00:02:48].

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Reading the carrier's Xactimate estimate starts with simple math. Builder's Perspective Public Adjusting divides the roof sketch area by 100, so 2,901.94 SF becomes 29.02 squares, and then compares tear-off quantity to roof area: when they match, the carrier is agreeing to full replacement, while something like 0.33 squares means “one bundle of shingles to repair your roof basically” [kWxJ6PIkM-M @ 00:04:42]. The same review caught water barrier membrane entered as 24.48 SF when it should have been 2,448 SF, which he fixes by multiplying the 21.61 unit price by 100 and calls likely an honest mistake [kWxJ6PIkM-M @ 00:06:15]. Chad Michael works the trade codes on the DFW price list, where drywall runs 0.46 to remove, 3.12 to replace, and 3.58 to R&R. His move is switching removal lines from DMO to the actual trade: drip edge removal goes from 0.36 to 0.96, drywall removal from 0.46 to 1.05, and shingle removal from 61.73 to about 150 [vkrXTVQcVQQ @ 00:18:23]. His first 20 attempts were all denied, and he now lands roughly 40 percent, 4 of 10, with the switch working on ESX submissions and with Nationwide while State Farm will not revise its own estimate [vkrXTVQcVQQ @ 00:13:50].

The adjuster meeting is run like a job site. Chris Zimmerman's truck kit is a ladder, tool bag, chalk, tape measure, shingle gauge, pitch gauge, and something to write on, and anything missing once stays in the truck permanently. On the roof he asks “What do you need from me?”, conversationally checks whether the adjuster has authority, is deciding or only documenting, and has seen the claim file, then raises unmarked damage before they finish [LwNOcenSP_c @ 00:02:07]. He closes with a recap in front of the homeowner, ideally on the Ring camera, pinning down peril causation and agreed counts such as eight wind damage shingles on the front and two on the left, because desk adjusters often contradict the field adjuster [LwNOcenSP_c @ 00:04:38]. Chad Michael's inspection standard is every room, closet, and hallway, at least 2 hours, both owners present, and 2 to 3 appointments a day instead of 8, with 200 to 300 photos plus drone footage handed to the client in a Google Drive folder [vkrXTVQcVQQ @ 00:34:49]. When an adjuster piles on paperwork, Zimmerman's script is “is this a recommendation or is this a requirement?”, and if it is a requirement, ask what it is based on [9A5QEe9xxXk @ 00:01:21].

The negotiation itself is short and the money math is blunt. Shane O'Dazier, who starts from the premise that adjusters are obligated “to not overpay,” abandoned the hour of phone-tag line-by-line argument that used to cut a 25-line estimate in half, $6K to $3K or $8K to $4K, and now collects every adjuster question first without arguing, totals them, and finishes in 3 to 4 minutes [3xfQ7PdL-AA @ 00:06:10]. His rule is to accept up to 10 percent off, refuse anything deeper, collect the undisputed amount, and back it with an attorney-fee provision clause, with his front desk holding authority to accept reductions [3xfQ7PdL-AA @ 00:07:49]. On the PA side, Vince Perri quotes fees of 10, 15, or 20 percent, says it is no issue in 9 of 10 cases, and otherwise the contractor absorbs the loss or adjusts commission to keep the deal alive [RRn3mzn9xCw @ 00:15:09]. American Roof Supplements prices its outsourced estimating work for contractors at a free first estimate or supplement, $50 for a pre-adjuster estimate, $100 for a follow-up supplement on the same approved job, and $150 standalone, with no monthly fee or minimum and PAs paying the same [zDKvQs0viSI @ 00:10:20].

sop_steps.title: Decode the carrier estimate
sop_steps.action: Convert sketch area to squares, test tear-off against roof area, and hunt unit errors.
sop_steps.detail: Divide square footage by 100, treat a tear-off matching roof area as full replacement, and flag entries like a 24.48-square tear-off that is likely the entire roof or membrane entered at 24.48 SF instead of 2,448 SF [Builder's Perspective Public Adjusting — kWxJ6PIkM-M @ 00:05:53]

sop_steps.title: Rebuild the line items with trade codes and proof
sop_steps.action: Switch DMO removal codes to the actual trade and attach a photo, code, and footnote to each item.

sop_steps.title: Run the adjuster meeting and recorded recap
sop_steps.action: Arrive with the full kit, ask what the adjuster needs, raise unmarked damage, then recap with the homeowner.
sop_steps.detail: Confirm peril causation, substantial damage, and agreed counts such as eight wind damage shingles on the front and two on the left, ideally on the Ring camera [Chris Zimmerman — LwNOcenSP_c @ 00:05:20]

sop_steps.action: Collect every adjuster question without arguing, total the cuts, and apply the 10 percent rule.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split at the negotiation table is whether to settle at all. Chad Michael draws a hard line: never agree to settle with an insurance company, no matter where the claim sits in the process, and when an adjuster at $20K revises toward $30K against a $40K contractor number, the script is 'I can't agree to anything... send the money,' because an estimate is only a prediction of the future and the contractor holds the power [vkrXTVQcVQQ @ 00:00:59]. claimhelpme also rejects bargaining, stating 'I don't believe in negotiations' and pointing to the New York DFS definition of a public adjuster, yet still calls an informed settlement acceptable after watching $90K of repairs plus $20K of pack-out resolve for about $40K with a homeowner who was happy [2WVlG5yPBTU @ 00:02:01]. Shane O'Dazier runs a pragmatic middle playbook: the shop accepts reductions up to 10 percent, refuses anything deeper, collects the undisputed amount, and gives the front desk authority to approve cuts inside that band [3xfQ7PdL-AA @ 00:06:23]. The Roofing Insights panel supplies the counterweight, with one panelist stating flatly that insurance companies do make reasonable settlements, so walling off every carrier number is not universal doctrine [uykTx34p0Js @ 00:09:53].

The second fault line is who sits across from the adjuster and who gets cut out. Vince Perri, running Elite Resolutions across Florida, Texas, North Carolina and California, lays out the Florida split: a contractor may suggest filing a claim and discuss a bid for usual and customary fees but may not negotiate, while a public adjuster puts more money in the client's pocket '10 times out of 10' [RRn3mzn9xCw @ 00:09:10]. Avner Gat goes further against restorers, warning that restoration companies offering to negotiate are not equipped, that clients call once those talks get stuck, and that 'You need a license in order to do that' [8x3Gfr6Uyr8 @ 00:02:41]. Anissa Coy of FirehouseEducation flips the whole premise: the restorer's real client is the insurer, bringing in a PA risks losing insurer work, and the restorer should never deal with the PA, only with the homeowner and the claims adjuster [GhZSitNz6aQ @ 00:05:11]. Mike of Repair King on Roofing Insights runs the reverse order of operations, finding the contractor first as the 'mechanic' and letting the contractor pick the PA, after watching a PA take 10 percent and simply go to appraisal, something Mike could have done without the fee [uykTx34p0Js @ 00:03:50].

Fees split the room just as hard. In the Roofing Insights debate, the insurer-side lawyer argues a 10 percent PA fee leaves the insured unable to fully fix the damage, running a $20K roof with a $1K deductible and a $2K fee, though the same lawyer prefers a PA at 10 percent over a lawyer at 45 percent and proposes no PA fee on uncontested dollars, which the PA refuses at that pay level [Qv99F8pvYNU @ 00:02:31]. Host Dimmitri Lipinski calls 10 percent reasonable and 25 to 35 percent a ripoff, arguing that getting 10 percent more while paying 25 percent is not a gain, and holds up a $25,000 claim where a PA charged a $1,500 flat fee as a must-hire case [uykTx34p0Js @ 00:06:28]. Builder's Perspective Public Adjusting times the hire instead of fighting the rate, waiting for the insurer's paperwork so the homeowner avoids paying 10 percent on that initial check [kWxJ6PIkM-M @ 00:00:00]. On tooling, Shane O'Dazier walked away from Xactimate after more than 1,000 claims, calling it the devil's tools owned by an insurance company, while the Roofing Insights lawyer concedes Xactimate is not the be-all and points toward retail-price contracts [3xfQ7PdL-AA @ 00:04:10].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Estimate-level failures show up first. Shane O'Dazier reports that Xactimate plus detailed notes was garbage, with adjusters cutting at random; the old phone-tag process meant an hour of line-by-line argument, a typical 12 questions on a 25-line estimate, and totals sliced in half, $6K to $3K, $8K to $4K, $4K to $2K [3xfQ7PdL-AA @ 00:01:20]. Chad Michael's trade-code switch, moving items off DMO to the actual trade so drip edge removal jumps from 0.36 to 0.96 and drywall removal from 0.46 to 1.05, went 0 for 20 at first before climbing to roughly 4 approvals in 10, and State Farm still will not revise its own estimate [vkrXTVQcVQQ @ 00:13:23]. Builder's Perspective Public Adjusting caught a carrier entering water barrier membrane at 24.48 SF instead of 2,448 SF, a gap exposed by multiplying the 21.61 price by 100, and calls it likely an honest mistake, but one that still shorts the homeowner until someone reads the estimate line by line [kWxJ6PIkM-M @ 00:06:15]. claimhelpme adds that holding a license does not mean a PA understands construction or estimating, and that an unchallenged low carrier number becomes the baseline everyone negotiates from [2WVlG5yPBTU @ 00:00:57].

The legal tripwires land on the contractor's paper. John Black of Daly & Black lists the Texas UPPA functions, investigating, appraising, evaluating or advocating, preparing or negotiating the claim, advising on policy terms, and advertising as an adjuster, and says the permission or power-of-attorney workaround is barred by Texas Insurance Code section 4102.163; the result is a void contract, a policyholder who can refuse to pay, and a contractor left holding the bag [jaGktNyKvE4 @ 00:02:12]. Building Experts Institute targets the classic contingency line, 'We will do the work for the amount the insurance company approves,' as negotiating the claim outcome, likely illegal anyway for lacking a set dollar consideration, and functioning as an assignment of benefits in states without one; the fix is a stated scope and price, a cancellation clause if the insurer does not approve in full, and a change order on partial approval [RmjqTZJ3II0 @ 00:00:20]. American Roof Supplements reminds contractors that a roofing contract does not authorize representing the insured and that Texas regulators warn contractors against acting as PAs [zDKvQs0viSI @ 00:01:55]. Grossman PA LLC reviews invoices for attorneys where homeowners are pursued for unpaid restoration bills years later, because the homeowner's name sits on the contract [diiBgujlZF0 @ 00:01:02].

Adjuster behavior and the money math create the rest of the losses. Chris Zimmerman reads an Auto-Owners demand for a city-inspector form across 64 townhouse units, over crickets and chimney flashing after a 5-day adjustment, as a claim-fatigue tactic, since getting the city to fill it out could take 3 to 6 months; even a city-page screenshot showing 2021 IRC enforcement was refused [9A5QEe9xxXk @ 00:04:03]. Zimmerman also warns that field adjusters' statements often get contradicted by the desk adjuster, which is why the recap happens with the homeowner, preferably on the Ring camera, locking in agreed counts like eight wind-damaged shingles on the front and two on the left [LwNOcenSP_c @ 00:04:38]. Grossman PA LLC flags the inflation trap from the carrier-review side: a $7,500 job paid directly by a homeowner gets billed to the insurer at $10,000 to $20,000, and reviews surface duplicate charges, unsupported labor, unnecessary equipment and outsourced estimates the contractor cannot explain [diiBgujlZF0 @ 00:01:31]. On Roofing Insights, Mike warns depreciation is released only after the work is complete, owners who claim 100 percent but do 20 percent get caught on later claims, and 15 of 18 properties handed to a big-name PA produced zero results [uykTx34p0Js @ 00:17:15].

callout.title: Four checks before you sit at the negotiation table
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, reversal, or trap the practitioners hit or watched others hit on live claims.
items: Rewrite any 'we will do the work for the amount the insurance company approves' contract into a stated scope and price with a cancellation clause and a change order for partial approval [Building Experts Institute — RmjqTZJ3II0 @ 00:01:19].
Do not lean on homeowner permission or a power of attorney to negotiate in Texas; section 4102.163 bars it and leaves the contractor holding the bag [Daly & Black, P.C. — jaGktNyKvE4 @ 00:01:55].
Calendar proof-of-loss the day of the loss, because deadlines run 60 days and can be as short as 30 [The Adjuster's Roundtable — _wmRAji2ZmI @ 00:08:35].
Before complying with any extra adjuster demand, ask whether it is a recommendation or a requirement, and if required, ask what it is based on [Chris Zimmerman — 9A5QEe9xxXk @ 00:01:21].

chapters.pull_quote: 'A weak estimate creates a weak starting point.' — claimhelpme (2WVlG5yPBTU @ 00:03:46).
action_checklist: List every adjuster question first without arguing, total them up, and close the call in 3 to 4 minutes instead of an hour of line-item fights [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — 3xfQ7PdL-AA @ 00:05:41].
Attach a photo, a code citation, and an 'add item info note' footnote to every Xactimate line, using 'item image' to show what is included [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — vkrXTVQcVQQ @ 00:06:44].

Convert the roof sketch to squares (2,901.94 SF divided by 100 equals 29.02 squares) and check whether tear-off matches roof area to confirm full replacement [Builder's Perspective Public Adjusting — kWxJ6PIkM-M @ 00:03:57].

Open the adjuster roof walk by asking 'What do you need from me?' and confirm authority, claim-file review, covered peril, and estimate status conversationally [Chris Zimmerman — LwNOcenSP_c @ 00:02:07].
Shoot the overall slope before detail, include a measurement in frame, and label every photo [American Roof Supplements — zDKvQs0viSI @ 00:02:50].

On a denial, bring in vetted experts, prepare rebuild estimates, and present a full documentation package, escalating to upper management when desk adjusters hold their position [The Adjuster's Roundtable — _wmRAji2ZmI @ 00:02:48].

chapters.question_prompt: What are third-party administrators and carrier-directed programs, how do contractors get on them, and what are the risks of the insurer's preferred vendor?
chapters.title: TPAs, Carrier Programs, and Preferred Vendors
chapters.subtitle: Getting on TPA lists, winning the Contractor Connections and Alacrity game, Sedgwick claim handling and training, TPA licensure, healthcare and self-funded TPA models, types of adjusters including remote desk adjusters, and why homeowners avoid insurance-company contractors
chapters.executive_summary: Restoration operators agree that third-party administrators now sit between contractors and carriers. Jon Schoen says very few adjusters still work for insurers, and The DYOJO host puts the TPA share at upwards of 80% of claims. Programs such as Contractor Connection bundle 30 to 40 carriers, each requiring separate approval. They charge contractors a 5 to 10% fee and impose a preset, discounted price list with no markup. The street mechanics are dictated: a day-stamped report sets dehu and air-mover counts, a 3-day drying cap applies, Xactimate is mandatory and documentation is uploaded twice. David Smith says he never lost a documented dispute and that a program can hand over a $250,000 fire nobody chased. Brian Close counters that guaranteed work is not always profitable, and public adjusters attack preferred vendors as volume shops that shortchange policyholders.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The restoration operators agree on the first fact of this market: the carrier adjuster is no longer the gatekeeper. Jon Schoen puts it flatly: 'very few adjusters now work for the insurance companies and most of their work goes through third- party administrators.' He traces the shift to TPAs offering to run claims for free while carriers cut adjuster headcount [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:04:23]. On The DYOJO panel, the host put the TPA share at upwards of 80% of claims. He quoted growth from 1.21B to 271B across 2010 to 2020 [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:19:10]. Schoen stresses that a program is not one door but dozens. Contractor Connection alone holds 30 to 40 carriers, including USAA, Nationwide, State Farm and Allstate, and a contractor must win approval from each carrier inside each program [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:01:00]. Sylvia Browy draws the same line from the adjuster side. She describes Sedgwick as a TPA that handles claims for others and sells no policies, in contrast to State Farm as a direct carrier [u947iwIhI7A @ 00:00:41]. The operating consequence is simple. Anyone running mitigation or repairs is negotiating with an administrator whose client is the carrier. Every approval, rotation slot and price list is set at that administrative layer, not at the homeowner's kitchen table.

Every restoration voice agrees that the volume carries a toll. Schoen states the TPA will 'charge the contractor 5 10%' to do the work. On top of that sits a preset, discounted price list with line items removed: 'their price list is is preset you can't change it.' Outside programs, he marks the standard list up 20% [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:07:43]. Ty Penzone, a Washington repair contractor with 20-plus years in the trade, says the same thing in fewer words: 'the line items are what the line items are' [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:16:04]. Brian Close of American Restoration runs recon only and stays off programs. He frames program work as guaranteed work that is 'not always guaranteed to be profitable,' the fallback an owner reaches for before bankruptcy [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:02:58]. Schoen adds the sharpest edge. Even inside a program, 'you're still not guaranteed to get paid,' and a homeowner can walk off with the money [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:04:45]. The baseline prerequisite is margin discipline. A shop entering programs must price its overhead against a 5 to 10 percent fee, a frozen list with no markup, and collection risk the program does not absorb. Operators who cannot run lean on those terms are buying volume with their own balance sheet.

The third consensus point is documentation. It comes from the mitigation side as hard as from the repair side. David Smith, an Oregon mitigation owner with 11 years in, says reviewer pushback means you lack documentation, and that he never lost a dispute he had documented [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:37:35]. His rule is 'documentation, documentation, documentation, regardless of where your work is coming from.' That holds whether the end user is a carrier, a reviewer or a homeowner, because you will have to explain the reason for your repair process [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:48:01]. Schoen gets specific about what program reviewers want to see: moisture readings must show specific humidity dropping [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:08:21]. Ty Penzone treats the relationship as a partnership rather than a vendor transaction, and the panel credits TPAs with partnering with contractors straight through COVID [onSDIprTeAU @ 01:03:47]. The prerequisites the operators agree on stack up in order. First comes a local foundation before chasing programs. Next is a willingness to learn both the program's rules and each carrier's rules, plus admin capacity for duplicate uploads and estimating. Last is the habit of logging every reading and photo as if the file will be argued.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Getting on a list is a sales campaign, not an application. Schoen's playbook starts with applying to every program, expecting to pay a fee, and accepting there is no guarantee of placement. The opening comes when an incumbent underperforms in a territory and the 'switch flips' [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:10:19]. The next move is relationship work. Get the regional manager's name and number, introduce yourself, and invite them to walk your facility and inspect your equipment. In his words, it is 'very important to have the regional manager's name and number so you can introduce yourself' [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:11:42]. He also works the field side by having adjusters and agents push for the company. That push lands hardest when claim volume is high and the program needs capacity [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:12:01]. David Smith's addition is commitment. Once inside, learn both the program requirements and the carrier requirements, because both rule sets apply to the same file [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:12:23]. The sequence matters. Applications sit dormant until a slot opens. The regional manager decides who fills that slot, and adjuster and agent advocacy tips the decision. Whether a contractor stays on the list once the switch flips depends on mastering two rulebooks.

Inside the program, the drying math is dictated rather than negotiated. Schoen describes the 'micia' report, timestamped day by day, which sets dehumidifier and air-mover counts that can fall below S500. If the room calls for a small dehu, you are paid for a small even if you placed a large [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:06:02]. David Smith sees contractors overshoot in the other direction. They set '45 D HUs and 75 fans in two rooms' and then do not get paid for it [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:44:40]. The paperwork load is a fixed cost to plan for. Documentation must be uploaded twice, once to your own system and once to the program, though some CRMs auto-upload [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:05:23]. Xactimate is mandatory and a second software platform may be required. Schoen tells owners to either train admin staff or sub the paperwork out [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:06:42]. The practical read is direct. Set equipment to match what the program's report will pay. Log readings daily to show specific humidity dropping, and keep estimating in Xactimate from the first visit forward. Shops that set equipment by feel end up arguing with a reviewer over gear they already paid to haul in, run and pull back out.

The economics reward speed and volume rather than per-job margin. Schoen describes somewhat regular job flow through rotation, scored on arrival speed and direct customer reviews. He is blunt that you are 'going to pay 5 10% a fee to be on the program' [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:08:41]. He adds that mitigation pays well while construction is harder [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:09:17]. The program wars show what TPAs actually sell to carriers. Alacrity won Nationwide by promising $5M a year in savings, with no roughly $100 setup fee and no $150 service-call fee. Contractor Connection took the account back with a 3-day drying cap it pitched as $20M in savings [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:03:50]. Each of those savings is a line the contractor no longer bills. Ty Penzone explains how repair shops still make the channel work: subs accept lower rates in exchange for year-round volume [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:55:23]. Put the numbers together and the model is clear. Arrival speed and reviews win the rotation, and mitigation carries the margin while construction fights the list. Every dollar a TPA promises a carrier comes out of fees and drying days the contractor used to control. The model only works when crews and subs stay busy enough to spread the fee across many files.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Program work versus going direct is the sharpest split on the restoration side. Jon Schoen sits on Contractor Connection, Alacrity, and Sedgwick and still frames the deal as a toll: the TPA charges the contractor 5 to 10% to do the work, the price list is preset and discounted, and outside the programs Schoen marks the standard list up 20% instead [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:02:35]. Brian Close of American Restoration runs recon only and stays off the programs, calling program volume guaranteed work that is 'not always guaranteed to be profitable' and the fallback a shop reaches for right before bankruptcy [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:02:58]. David Smith, eleven years into Oregon mitigation, pushes back hard: a program can hand you a $250,000 fire you never chased, and the payoff only comes if you commit and learn both the program rules and each carrier's requirements [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:11:17]. Ty Penzone, twenty-plus years in Washington repairs, reports that going direct demanded heavy marketing spend, so the real choice is sweat equity plus some financial outlay, or more financial outlay and less sweat [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:33:09]. David's own sequencing is the practical middle path: build a local direct foundation first, then run program and direct channels side by side.

The second fault line is whether a carrier's preferred vendor is a partner or a liability. Mike of The Claim Squad Public Adjusters calls preferred vendors beginners grinding volume on thin margins who get dropped if they treat policyholders fairly, and tells homeowners to answer the intake question 'Do you need water mitigation?' by declining and naming their own vendor [h_W9kUbadMM @ 00:03:07]. On-Site Adjusting goes further, warning that the insurer's contractor removes and dumps evidence before coverage is even decided, so an attorney, public adjuster, or engineer should be on site within days [oEc6cQdcK6I @ 00:00:32]. The DYOJO panel tells the opposite story from inside the network: when Ty Penzone's own house burned in 2008, a network vendor did the repair [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:34:09]. Chris Zimmerman adds a contractor's warning about the public adjuster route itself: once a letter of representation lands, the insurer stops talking to the contractor, the homeowner risks getting ghosted, cancelling the letter is difficult, and the result may cost more and turn out worse [esg8I0BJFLM @ 00:05:18]. Zimmerman also stresses that bringing in a public adjuster is the homeowner's decision and belongs on the table only once a claim has stalled.

The third split is how much leverage anyone has against the administrator's paper. On the repair side, one DYOJO voice shrugs that 'the line items are what the line items are' [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:16:04], while David Smith insists reviewer pushback only means the file lacks documentation and reports never losing a documented dispute [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:37:35]. The benefits-plan practitioners fight the same war over contracts. The independent-TPA voice on Chris Hamilton's channel argues that shifting administrators 'shouldn't be at all that difficult' and that brokers who renew a bundled solution for 20-plus years are hitting the easy button [LEzohuG5ykg @ 00:02:28]. Claire Brockbank of 32BJ, running about 200,000 lives, paints a harder picture: bad contracts block program exits, force upside-down claims, and cede data ownership, and even after a disciplined RFP a buyer should expect to win roughly a third of the asks [pNIYu-t990E @ 00:31:59]. The 32BJ alternative playbook is to send the RFP with the buyer's own contract, demand a redline in every response, plant parallel 'Easter egg' questions to catch sales and legal contradictions, and play Aetna, United, and Anthem against each other whenever one calls an ask 'not industry practice.' Both camps land on the same lever: owning the data and the documentation.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap is placing equipment the program will not pay for. Jon Schoen explains that the micia report is timestamped day by day and dictates dehumidifier and air-mover counts, possibly below S500, so if the room calls for a small dehu you are paid for a small even when you placed a large [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:06:02]. The caps come straight from TPA sales pitches to carriers: Alacrity won Nationwide by promising $5M a year in savings by dropping the roughly $100 setup fee and $150 service-call fee, and Contractor Connection won the account back with a three-day drying cap claiming $20M in savings [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:03:50]. David Smith sees contractors set '45 D HUs and 75 fans in two rooms' and then get nothing for it [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:44:40]. Schoen's readings rule closes the loop: the logs must show specific humidity dropping day over day [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:08:21]. Even when the file is clean, Schoen warns payment is still not guaranteed, because a homeowner can walk away with the money. The economics check is simple: run the job to the program's equipment math and drying window, not to your own habits, and log readings that prove every day billed.

The second trap is building a company whose survival depends on someone else's dispatch queue. Ty Penzone's flooring company ran 125 homes a year from 2002 to 2006 while charging retail clients 1.5 times, then fell to one job in a month in 2008 [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:56:46]. One DYOJO panelist puts it bluntly: 'I had a business that its entire solvency was built around doing 150 jobs a year plus' [onSDIprTeAU @ 00:59:09], which is why Ty argues for running diversified models to survive a 'model interrupt.' Back-office load is the quieter drain. Jon Schoen reports that documentation must be uploaded twice unless a CRM auto-uploads, that Xactimate is mandatory and a second software may be required, and that owners should plan to train admin staff or sub the paperwork out [-0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:06:42]. Joe Boyle of ClearFile sees the same scheduling trap from the administrator's own licensing desk: approvals take one week to three months, renewals cluster January through March, and financials must be current within 30 to 60 days, so step one is 'a very modest timeline' [kR0zavFV0HU @ 00:02:38]. Underestimating paperwork time, on either side of the TPA relationship, quietly kills margin and deadlines.

The third trap is signing or working under paper nobody read. On Relentless Health Value, 32BJ's Claire Brockbank and host Stacey Richter peg about 95% of employers as deferring to the TPA's paper and losing rights in fine print like a 'footnote on page 78,' because 'very few of us have contracting expertise, so we accept the language' [pNIYu-t990E @ 00:06:09]. The cost was concrete: upside-down claims ran 32BJ about $10M in one year, with a $100 bill paid at $200, and the typical failure has sales overpromising, lawyers retracting, and contracting still open a year into implementation [pNIYu-t990E @ 00:04:19]. Their rule after signing is 'You have to police this.' On the claims side, Leah Small of Chisholm Chisholm & Kilpatrick reports that Sedgwick recommends approval or denial without paying benefits, often aims to minimize payouts, and leans on file reviews instead of exams so treating physicians get dismissed [lnhw4pYCOFU @ 00:01:29]. The fatal mistake is a thin appeal: in most cases no new evidence is allowed after the appeal closes, so every denial basis has to be rebutted with vocational reports, symptom journals, and physician reports up front [lnhw4pYCOFU @ 00:02:54]. Whether the counterparty is a plan buyer or a claimant, losing the record early is losing the fight.

callout.title: Stop Before You Sign the Paper or Place a Single Dehu
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, cut, or collapse the practitioners lived through or watched happen. Clear all four before taking program volume or signing an administrator's contract.
items: Pull the program's micia equipment counts before placing dehus and air movers, because an oversized unit gets paid as the small one the room called for [Water Damage Restoration Coach - Jon Schoen — -0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:06:02].

Confirm Xactimate seats and any second software, and decide whether to train admin staff or sub the paperwork out before the first program job lands [Water Damage Restoration Coach - Jon Schoen — -0hAYhkhJaw @ 00:06:42].
Model the business so no single channel carries solvency; a shop built around 150 jobs a year plus collapsed to one job a month in 2008 [The DYOJO — onSDIprTeAU @ 00:59:09].

Redline the administrator's contract before signing and police vendor compliance afterward, because the fine print is where exits and data ownership disappear [Relentless Health Value — pNIYu-t990E @ 00:34:31].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I handle fire, smoke, and contents jobs, and which documentation and scanning tools support the scope?
chapters.title: Fire, Smoke, Contents, and Job-Site Documentation
chapters.subtitle: Packout vs. clean-in-place, packout for ultrasonic processing, wildfire smoke-damaged contents, smoke odor removal, a fire project manager's perspective, the Encircle fire and smoke bootcamp, scope sheets, magicplan water documentation, Matterport and Leica RTC scanning, Encircle scope-to-estimate, outsourcing PA estimates, and lead-safe interior containment
chapters.executive_summary: Fire and contents operators converge on one rule: you get paid for what you document. Encircle's Paul Donald, Octagon's Brendy Riley, and bootcamp instructor Chris all tie payment to defensible photos, scans, and narratives built from the first site visit, while FirehouseEducation and Omegasonics treat a digital photo inventory as the floor for every packout. The street mechanics are concrete: Matterport scans placed 5-8 ft apart at 4-4.5 ft height, sponge tests on 1 ft x 1 ft squares, AFDs sized for 6-8 air changes per hour, bubble wrap billed at twenty dollars a box, and AI scopes that turn a voice description into a priced Xactimate file in under 20 minutes. The splits are sharp: ozone versus hydroxyl, Matterport accuracy versus Leica RTC point clouds, Encircle's own 2-5% versus 5-10% revenue-lift claims, and outsourced estimating versus doing it yourself.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator who talks money ties it back to the file. Encircle CEO Paul Donald frames the whole business in one line: restoration contractors "only get paid for the work they document," and without defensible data, AI is just "a creative tool generating a plausible story" [uy09gaqf4AU @ 00:03:46]. Octagon project manager Brendy Riley lived that on a 7,000 sq ft ski-resort retirement home where a stain rag combusted over a weekend; the smoke path stayed invisible until drywall came off, engineers reviewed the estimates, and the team still got paid for the correct scope because they had "the photo documentation to justify it and the knowledge on how to convey that" [WTz841eMFkk @ 00:11:32]. Bootcamp instructor Chris pushes the same logic upstream: set the restoration objective at the start, the way you would a drying plan, because "if you establish the objective at the beginning then it makes it easier to get paid at the end" [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 00:05:10]. On the mitigation side, magicplan sells floor-plan sketches exported straight to Xactimate specifically to "expedite your payment process and ensure full compensation," replacing pen-and-paper sketches with a mobile app that carries photos, moisture readings and signatures in one project [irpHqZ46CG8 @ 00:05:00].

On contents, the FirehouseEducation crew gives the cleanest decision rule: medium to heavy fire, or anything needing ultrasonic work, gets packed out to the warehouse, while light smoke is cleaned in place to avoid expense and hassle [w85_KBcX690 @ 00:00:49]. Even a light job flips to a partial packout when the structure needs paint or carpet, and the deciding factors are degree of damage, need for ultrasonic, intensity of cleaning and structural damage. Omegasonics' Frank Pedu sets the floor for every packout: a digital photo inventory is the minimum because it "protects you from fraudulent claims and misplaced contents," and each item's original condition and final storage location must be recorded [3UmvqUcOFDc @ 00:01:09]. Annissa Coy is blunter: inventory everything on insurance claims [MkCNqNRsk04 @ 00:12:04]. Chris adds the money angle on pre-cleaning: HEPA-vacuuming contents before they ever hit a box raises the save percentage, and since there is no industry labeling standard, Chris's convention is white boxes for clean and brown boxes for dirty [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 03:47:03]. The shared baseline is that contents are not loaded and forgotten; every piece leaves the house photographed, categorized, pre-cleaned where soot is heavy, and assigned to a known storage spot.

The cleaning sequence is where the fire specialists line up hardest. Chris teaches four steps of fire remediation, "Source removal cleaning deodorization and then applying surface sealant," with the effort front-loaded, and warns that most disputes come from attacking odor before contaminants are gone [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 02:10:13]. Brendy Riley's field workflow at Octagon mirrors it: environmental controls first to stop soot and carcinogens resettling, then demo, media blasting depending on char level and the clean-versus-replace call, then HEPA vacuum, chem sponge and damp wipe, odor mitigation throughout, and finally a fire and smoke sealer, where "usually it takes one to two applications to mitigate any lingering odors" [WTz841eMFkk @ 00:04:03]. Travis Chauncey of Abbotts explains why the HEPA step is non-negotiable: smoke particulates run under 10 microns, so a regular shop vac will not capture them [iiCSRcut-WA @ 00:01:33]. Annissa Coy carries that into contents, HEPA-vacuuming before boxing, especially under heavy soot, and unpacking only inside the processing center under a HEPA scrubber [MkCNqNRsk04 @ 00:01:37]. Chris puts it flatly elsewhere: the most effective removal is physical, not hydroxy. The consensus baseline: physical removal first, deodorize second, seal last, on a clean, dry surface as the sealer label itself requires.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Adjuster TV's walkthrough with Kylee Kempton of Titan Restoration in Mesa gives the tightest scan protocol. Water technicians carry a Matterport in every truck, shoot a pre-scan before mitigation and a post-scan after demolition, so the adjuster sees removed versus to-repair work, with Mattertags carrying loss descriptions and quantities [86mEe0yHwiw @ 00:06:43]. The capture rules: place scans 5 to 8 ft apart, hold the camera at about 4 to 4.5 ft for restoration rather than eye level, hide behind it to avoid "no alignment" errors, scan just before and after doorways, close blinds so sunlight does not confuse the infrared, mark mirrors early and often, open doors to 45 degrees, and add 2 to 3 extra scans in tight bathrooms [86mEe0yHwiw @ 00:13:42]. For under-sink losses, open the cabinets and drop the tripod to its lowest height. The magicplan workflow layers moisture data on the sketch: insert a restoration humidity and temperature object, drag it onto the annotated humid zone, and log surface and air humidity, date and photos as custom attributes [irpHqZ46CG8 @ 00:04:10]. On paper, Adjusterpedia's Mark runs a coded scope sheet because photos alone led to mislabeling and confusion over what was actually damaged [4EdiIO_RCX0 @ 00:00:55].

The estimating pipeline is where the minutes get won. In Encircle's demo, the technician dictates a damage description by voice, adds photos, 360s, video, moisture and equipment data, and the platform outputs a narrative, room tasks and IICRC-backed equipment calculations in 5 to 10 minutes [uy09gaqf4AU @ 00:12:32]. In Xactimate, the operator files a vendor data request, matches the claim ID, and sends; AI converts the sketch and maps tasks to line items priced from the price list chosen when the project was created. Joe's live run, a 15x12x8 Category 1 bedroom with carpet saved, pad pulled and a 9x3 hallway of wet hardwood, took about 30 to 60 seconds to describe and produced a priced estimate in under 20 minutes [uy09gaqf4AU @ 00:37:55]. David Herring's field number backs the voice-note method: 998 windows inspected in 3 days versus about 7 the old way, and Herring calls line items produced in the field "a disservice" [uy09gaqf4AU @ 00:22:42]. For firms that would rather hand off the Xactimate build entirely, American Roof Supplements publishes flat pricing: first estimate or supplement free, $50 pre-adjuster estimate, $100 follow-up supplement on a job they estimated and got approved, $150 standalone supplement, no monthly fee or minimum [GK_Was-iK98 @ 00:09:42].

Packout and cleaning carry their own unit economics. FirehouseEducation treats materials as billable, charged hourly or built into the per-box price, with bubble wrap running about "twenty dollars a box" and the instruction "don't skimp"; specialty TV, lamp, dish-pack and glass-pack boxes come out, plates go on end, dish packs bill higher, and wood gets paper-wrapped before shrink wrap in hot areas [rAAR3Zmm80c @ 00:01:53]. That crew credits the method with very little damage over 16 to 17 years. In the processing center, Annissa Coy runs dishes and dippable items through an ultrasonic with a pre-soak because it is faster "and thus profitable," handles dry-method items with HEPA plus a dry sponge or art gum eraser, and deodorizes with hydroxyl inside the drying chamber [MkCNqNRsk04 @ 00:06:42]. Chris quantifies the structure side: verify cleaning with a 1 ft by 1 ft sponge test using horizontal and vertical passes, size air filtration for 6 to 8 air changes per hour then drop to 4, targeting 2,000 particles at 3 microns, with particle counts like 13,000 down to 500 as proof [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 01:36:28]. Heat-calcined drywall cannot be rehydrated, so replace it at $8 to $16 a sheet, which Chris frames as an extra $4 [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 02:31:11].

callout.title: What the crews do that rookies skip
callout.body: Small field habits the practitioners use to protect scans, odor results, and fragile contents.
items: Drop the Matterport tripod to its lowest height and open the cabinets for under-sink water losses, and add 2 to 3 extra scans in tight bathrooms to cover the tripod blind spot [Adjuster TV — 86mEe0yHwiw @ 00:23:01].

Never let the homeowner do the laundry on a smoke job; it obscures the source of any remaining odor, so run it in-house or through a certified vendor, not "Suzy's Wash and Fold" [FirehouseEducation — MkCNqNRsk04 @ 00:09:05].
Send a second PM through the house for a "fresh nose" odor assessment before the final walkthrough [Octagon Cleaning and Restoration — WTz841eMFkk @ 00:06:35].

On a floor mirror, unscrew the 3-piece legs, box them in custom cardboard, blanket the mirror, shrink-wrap the legs to it and add a fragile sticker, because the loaded pod tilts high [FirehouseEducation — Appti0ctcGA @ 00:04:17].

sop_steps.title: Scan and sketch on arrival
sop_steps.action: Hit the site fast, prep the rooms, and pre-scan the loss before mitigation touches it.
sop_steps.detail: Site visit within the first 24 hours with an estimate goal of 48 hours; set lights on, curtains closed and doors positioned, then pre-scan before mitigation and post-scan after demo so the adjuster can compare removed versus to-repair work [Adjuster TV — 86mEe0yHwiw @ 00:03:32].

sop_steps.title: Dictate the scope narrative
sop_steps.action: Describe the damage by voice and attach photos, 360s, moisture and equipment data.
sop_steps.detail: The platform returns a narrative, room tasks and IICRC-backed equipment calculations in 5 to 10 minutes, then a vendor data request matched by claim ID pushes it into Xactimate for line-item pricing [Encircle — uy09gaqf4AU @ 00:12:32].

sop_steps.title: Decide packout and inventory contents
sop_steps.action: Choose full packout, partial packout, or clean in place, and photo-inventory every item.
sop_steps.detail: Weigh degree of damage, need for ultrasonic, intensity of cleaning and structural damage; pack out medium to heavy fire, clean light smoke in place, and go partial when paint or carpet work is coming [FirehouseEducation — w85_KBcX690 @ 00:01:39].

sop_steps.title: Clean, verify, then deodorize and seal
sop_steps.action: Remove residue physically, prove it with a sponge test, then deodorize and seal.
sop_steps.detail: Run a 1 ft by 1 ft sponge test with horizontal and vertical passes; the post-clean pass should come up clean before any deodorization or sealer goes on [Encircle — 33iGNdZ6fyE @ 00:45:37].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Odor control is the sharpest split. Annissa Coy at FirehouseEducation bans ozone outright on contents with an "absolutely not," because it bleaches anything damp and takes years off leather. Coy runs hydroxyl inside the drying chamber instead, since it is safe for occupants and works on wet goods [MkCNqNRsk04 @ 00:06:05]. Chris, the umpire-appraiser teaching Encircle's bootcamp, reverses that ranking. On protein fires Chris rates ozone above hydroxy and calls hydroxy three to four times weaker. Chris still holds that the most effective removal is physical, not hydroxy, and warns that whoever over-oxidizes a house owns the result [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 02:59:48]. The lever Chris prefers was used by only 3 to 4 percent of attendees: fresh-air dilution. The reasoning is that bringing fresh air in carries less risk than applying another product [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 03:02:49]. Travis Chauncey at Abbotts Cleanup & Restoration runs a homeowner-grade version. Open doors and windows, put positive air pressure in some areas and negative air machines in the affected ones, and move to demolition only if the odor persists [iiCSRcut-WA @ 00:00:43]. The working read is that contents crews lean toward hydroxyl, while structure-side dispute experts lean toward physical removal plus dilution. None of these operators treats an oxidizer as a substitute for actual cleaning.

The packout call is driven by damage load, not habit. Annissa Coy of FirehouseEducation sends medium to heavy fire jobs, and anything that needs ultrasonic work, to the warehouse. Light smoke gets cleaned in place to avoid the expense and hassle. Coy still runs a partial packout on light jobs when the structure needs paint or carpet work [w85_KBcX690 @ 00:00:49]. Coy's four decision factors are degree of damage, need for ultrasonic, intensity of cleaning, and structural damage. Coy states flatly that structural damage often forces the crew to pack contents up and get them out of the way so it can handle the structure [w85_KBcX690 @ 00:01:56]. Brendy Riley, a project manager with 11 years at Octagon, treats the packout as one line in a PM-run logistics stack. That stack also covers textile pickup, art restoration, and storage pods dropped on site. Riley keeps homeowners physically involved in moving items rather than icing them out [WTz841eMFkk @ 00:04:35]. Chris on the Encircle bootcamp argues that the save rate is decided before the truck is loaded, because HEPA pre-cleaning ahead of packout raises the percentage of items saved [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 03:47:03]. So the real disagreement is where the deep cleaning happens. Both camps HEPA the soot off before anything goes into a box.

The sharpest arguments over documentation tooling are about accuracy and about who structures the data. Kylee Kempton, the Matterport technician at Titan Restoration, pitches scanning as the cure for digging through 700 photos and making return trips to the site. Kempton claims correct scans are far more accurate than photos and that floor plans land within 1 to 2 percent [86mEe0yHwiw @ 00:04:07]. FirstLook Services runs Matterport and Leica RTC side by side and says accuracy is where Matterport falls off a cliff. In that firm's view Matterport is fine for quick-and-dirty floor plans and visuals but unfit for millimeter or centimeter construction documents, and mirrors throw phantom walls into Revit [C_iLoKezwu4 @ 00:01:16]. On the Encircle webinar, David Herring calls line items produced in the field a disservice. Herring argues for narrative damage descriptions instead and says they get about 90 percent more items cleared [uy09gaqf4AU @ 00:23:21]. Mark at Adjusterpedia still swears by a coded paper scope sheet printed on the back of the Xactanalysis claim info. Mark rejects separate roof, interior, and shed sheets as way too much, and insists that anyone skipping a scope sheet is probably not doing as good a job as possible [4EdiIO_RCX0 @ 00:00:19]. The playbooks diverge on capture medium but agree that structured input beats loose photos.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest failures come from letting someone else own the scope. Chris describes a loss of more than $600,000 in which an untrained adjuster changed the scope and the contractor followed it. The contractor ultimately was responsible, so the rule taught is never to take work instructions from the adjuster [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 00:09:57]. The same instructor saw a contractor seal odor into a senior home's roof without offering options, on a roughly $800,000 invoice, and the firm was left holding the bag [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 00:59:47]. Brendy Riley of Octagon answers with scope discipline set early. Build a hard scope with the adjuster upfront, raise new items the moment they appear so there are no surprises, and meet adjusters on site, since there may be several. On a 7,000-square-foot ski-resort home, a stain rag combusted over a weekend. The smoke path stayed invisible until the drywall came off, and engineers pushed back on the estimates. The crew still got paid for the correct scope, which Riley credits to having the photo documentation to justify it and the knowledge to convey it [WTz841eMFkk @ 00:11:32]. Chris's economics check matches that experience: establishing the objective at the beginning makes it easier to get paid at the end [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 00:05:10].

Chemistry mistakes cannot be undone, which is why practitioners treat them as economic traps rather than technique notes. Annissa Coy warns that you cannot ozone an item that is damp or wet, because it bleaches the goods and takes years off leather. Soft goods get no ozone at all [MkCNqNRsk04 @ 00:06:22]. Chris goes further on structures. Over-oxidation cannot be reversed, houses have ended up transferred to insurers because of it, and many cleaning-chemical labels already read "Do not expose to oxidizers" [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 02:59:48]. Protein fires are the other money pit, accounting for about 60 percent of Chris's disputes. The residue is invisible and tacky, it hardens like shellac within 24 to 72 hours, and oxidizers do little against it. Chris's warning is that protein fires are expensive, with no physical damage and simply a ton of cleaning [33iGNdZ6fyE @ 00:36:30]. Coy also forbids homeowner laundry on fire jobs, because it obscures the source of any remaining odor. Textiles go in-house or to a certified vendor rather than Suzy's Wash and Fold [MkCNqNRsk04 @ 00:09:05]. The common thread is that once a residue has been sealed, oxidized, or washed by the wrong hands, the restorer can no longer prove what is causing the lingering smell.

Packout and paperwork failures drain margin quietly. Annissa Coy and Jeremy of Faithful Restoration in Billings name the two classic packout losses: damage in transit, and cleaned items going dusty in storage and needing a second cleaning. Jeremy draws on 15 years at a furniture store plus moving labor. The fix is full shrink-wrap, moving blankets on corners, and taking pieces apart before loading, such as a floor mirror's three screw-in legs, because the pod tilts high once it is loaded [Appti0ctcGA @ 00:00:53]. Coy adds a heat trap: in hot areas, paper-wrap wood before the shrink wrap goes on. Coy also says never to skimp on billable materials, citing bubble wrap at about twenty dollars a box [rAAR3Zmm80c @ 00:03:46]. Frank Pedu at Omegasonics treats a digital photo inventory as the minimum, not the goal, because it protects the company from fraudulent claims and misplaced contents. Each item's original condition and final storage location should be logged [3UmvqUcOFDc @ 00:01:09]. On the estimating side, American Roof Supplements puts the public adjuster bottleneck at estimate number six. The firm treats late-night estimating, delayed follow-up, and turned-away files as signs of a capacity problem, and rejects handoffs that amount to forty photos and "figure it out" [GK_Was-iK98 @ 00:00:15].

callout.title: Stop-Points Before You Touch Contents or Chemistry
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, dispute or reversal practitioners reported firsthand. Clear all four before the crew commits labor or product.
items: Never discard an owner's belongings on your own call: you don't have the authority to throw people's stuff out, and it's not your job [Encircle — 33iGNdZ6fyE @ 01:20:22].
No ozone on anything damp or wet and none on soft goods, because it bleaches items and takes years off leather [FirehouseEducation — MkCNqNRsk04 @ 00:06:22].
Put high humidity in writing with thermo-hygrometer readings so a carrier that refused stabilization cannot later deny the mold [Encircle — 33iGNdZ6fyE @ 01:58:57].
On heat-damaged PEX, send a written no-warranty notice to both the homeowner and the adjuster, because the homeowner is the decision maker [Encircle — 33iGNdZ6fyE @ 03:49:52].

chapters.pull_quote: "If you've over oxidized it you own the result." — Chris, Encircle Fire & Smoke Restoration Bootcamp (33iGNdZ6fyE @ 03:00:25).
action_checklist: Open every loss in a floor-plan app under the client's last name, complete the project form (property type, age, cause, water category, date noticed, signature), and export the sketch to Xactimate [magicplan — irpHqZ46CG8 @ 00:01:33].

Take a 3D pre-scan before mitigation and a post-scan after demolition so the adjuster can compare removed work against to-repair work, with Mattertags carrying loss descriptions and quantities [Adjuster TV — 86mEe0yHwiw @ 00:06:43].

HEPA-vacuum heavy soot before boxing, then unpack only the day's work inside the processing center under a HEPA scrubber and bag wrap materials immediately [FirehouseEducation — MkCNqNRsk04 @ 00:01:37].
Log each item's original condition and final storage location in a digital photo inventory, packing by category with matched boxes [Omegasonics — 3UmvqUcOFDc @ 00:00:51].
Verify cleaning with a 1 ft by 1 ft sponge test using a horizontal and a vertical pass; the post-clean pass should come up clean [Encircle — 33iGNdZ6fyE @ 00:45:37].

Hand the estimating team an organized packet of measurements, photos, notes and carrier documents, then review the finished Xactimate file personally before it goes out [American Roof Supplements — GK_Was-iK98 @ 00:03:20].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I build a plumber referral network and convert more calls into signed water damage jobs?
chapters.title: The Plumber Referral Engine and Closing the Call
chapters.subtitle: Plumber referral programs, getting past gatekeepers, turning free dry-outs into $500K of referrals, alternatives to cash kickbacks, consistent jobs without storms, an agency lead-gen case study, call conversion tips, a sales system for sub-70% close rates, and selling from strength
chapters.executive_summary: Plumbers are the front door to water work. Jon Schoen calls them the number one referral source. Rowdy Legs of Homeway averaged six to ten jobs a week almost entirely from plumbers on the way to $11M, and Shane O'Dazier says the top companies dominate plumbers. The shared mechanic is discovery before pitch: find out what each service plumber wants, profile them in a CRM by fee band, and grow a referral tree to at least three jobs in 90 days. Street tools include the customer-posed shadow-plumber script, the $100-plus-$100-weekly slow-leak card, free dry-outs held to a 4:1 conversion ratio, CallRail whispers, and sub-60-minute arrival promises with 3-to-5-minute callbacks. The practitioners split hard on cash. Restorex pays percentage referral fees within a day, while Marketing Ninjas and Shane argue that cash builds no loyalty.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator here treats the plumber as the front door to water work. Jon Schoen built a 47-truck company and sold it. He calls plumbers the number one referral source because they see the job before the adjuster or agent ever does [HFcU3Nls6fM @ 00:00:01]. Restorex in Indianapolis says most of its business comes from referrals, and it frames plumbers as first on the scene [nFvUl2Kjwjs @ 00:00:21]. Shane O'Dazier goes further. Water and fire are the only gateway jobs, and the top restoration companies in any market are the ones that dominate plumbers [sUMKhFYRGSQ @ 00:09:01]. The proof case is Rowdy Legs of Homeway in Memphis. Rowdy learned the system from Shane and averaged six to ten jobs a week almost entirely from plumbers. Homeway went from zero to eleven million dollars in three years and only used internet marketing in the last six to eight months [Fj9S8rNJ5d4 @ 00:05:41]. The shared baseline is blunt: a restorer who cannot reliably pull jobs out of plumbing trucks is renting volume from storms and ad platforms. Every number in this chapter, from referral trees to close rates, sits downstream of that one acquisition skill. Practitioners treat the plumber channel as the base layer of a water company, not a side campaign run when the phones go quiet.

The second point of agreement is that you diagnose before you pitch. Shane's core rule is to find out what the plumber wants and give it to them. The options run from referral fees to leads to free tryouts, a combination, or none of those [D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:01:28]. Marketing Ninjas warns that walking in with a flyer or gift card attached to a pitch blows the visit. They use discovery questions instead, including asking about bad experiences the plumber has had with other restorers [n7ECptsaJTQ @ 00:00:26]. Shane learned this the hard way. Free dry-outs, swag, referral fees, breakfasts and a motorcycle giveaway all failed with the top plumber Shane chased. Every plumber is different, not all of them want free dry-outs, and some refuse referral fees outright [Rcmd8gVFzB8 @ 00:03:18]. Shane's phrase for the whole discipline is to use the right bait for the right fish [sUMKhFYRGSQ @ 00:01:13]. Guessing wrong is expensive. Shane says a wrong assumption flips a positive relationship negative fast. Unsolicited cash to a plumber who never asked for it tells them you are not different anymore. The consensus prerequisite is a documented answer, plumber by plumber, to one question: what actually moves this shop?

Practitioners also agree on who to target and on running the phone as a measured system. Shane tells operators not to judge a plumbing company by truck count. A one-truck service plumber sees leaks every day, while a twenty-truck construction outfit only sends warranty jobs. Target service over construction and residential over commercial. On commercial jobs a property manager controls the referral, and the contract has to be with the owner [D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:07:00]. Shane's criteria also include a minimum job volume per plumber and a less-is-more stance on how many relationships to run, all kept inside a tight county radius [xXe9Z763dDc @ 00:10:40]. Once referrals start ringing, Restoration Made Simple records every call through CallRail. Missed calls get caught, called back and used to train staff [8nQyv3vEI6A @ 00:02:50]. Albi's benchmark sets the bar for closing that call. A close rate under seventy percent means the company is missing a system, and the framework aims for seventy-five to eighty percent [mq8qI2hag0I @ 00:00:00]. Shane also advises staying out of multi-family and commercial policies for the first few years. The operator setup is a narrow list of residential service plumbers feeding a recorded, scripted phone line.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The prospecting engine starts with who you call and how you sound. Shane hunts what they call shadow plumbers, meaning shops absent from Google's front page. Plumbers who advertise want leads, while Google-Maps-only plumbers may be construction outfits [D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:16:59]. The call is made posing as a customer, not as a solicitor. Ask about relocating a water heater and a failed pop-off valve, then ask 'do y'all dry them out,' and follow a branching flowchart from whatever the plumber says [D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:19:05]. Every answer lands in a CRM plumber profile. The profile logs incentive preference and current fee in bands of under $300, $300, $500 and over $500. Call tracking is attached, and triangulating questions expose lies such as 'we don't refer anybody but want a referral fee' [D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:21:22]. When the plumber has no restorer, Shane runs the free leads play. Ask if they do this work, cover the area and want leads. Get a contact name, phone and email, and book an onboarding meeting, or simply send leads first. The non-negotiable is a backdoor contact, not the 1-800 number [ufmHlZ6tfKg @ 00:08:06]. Shane names the challenges the script has to solve: separating what a plumber wants from what they will take, differentiating, and landing the first job through servant marketing.

Incentives are built as specific instruments, not vague goodwill. Shane's slow leak play is a rebrand of the fake leak. It puts a real service call in front of the plumber's technician. In the example, the plumber was called to Joe's lake house for a sump pump and crawl space. Joe asked who the plumber calls for water damage and heard that the office calls somebody. Joe then handed over a card pre-loaded with $100, plus a $100 weekly drip [CV0x51fC7pw @ 00:02:34]. Joe replaces that sump pump every three to four years at $400 anyway and runs five consistent plumbers. Shane offers the drip only when the plumber already takes a fee elsewhere [MLuoMdYemWU @ 00:03:15]. Marketing Ninjas uses a fast-start bonus of double commission for thirty days [n7ECptsaJTQ @ 00:01:55]. Marketing Ninjas also runs a tier model in place of cash. After one referral the plumber gets priority dispatch, free dry-outs, dumpsters and shut-off tags with tracking numbers. After three, they get plumbing leads, co-branded materials and seasonal swag. After five, they get quarterly raffles, VIP access and training perks. After ten, they get team dinners, job-site banners, welcome boxes and a legacy wall [5Ibyq8oHR7Y @ 00:01:35]. Shane's timeline is about four weeks of incentivizing, which yields enough data to chase ideal fits instead of half-committed plumbers.

Closing the call is the back half of the engine. Restoration Made Simple sets a separate tracking number per site. A call whisper tells the answerer the source before they say hello, such as 'Denver North website lead' or 'plumbing referral 800 number' [8nQyv3vEI6A @ 00:04:29]. Their strategy four asks what city the caller is in, then relates with a shop fifteen minutes away or a tech in Littleton. Strategy eleven promises arrival in less than sixty minutes and a callback in three to five minutes, because a caller waiting on you is less likely to dial someone else. Their clients close ten to thirty percent more leads with these strategies [8nQyv3vEI6A @ 00:11:00]. Albi's phone rules are a scripted greeting, three qualifiers, no price ranges on the phone and no outsourced answering. On arrival that means a clean truck, a tucked shirt and street parking. On site, the ask is a crew within the next thirty minutes. The stronger ask is homeowner financing, or at least a deposit. An insurance objection gets a capped out-of-pocket cost with 0% APR for thirty-six months [mq8qI2hag0I @ 00:09:48]. Follow-up runs every twenty-four hours, and Albi reports that two of five leads lost at first close later with a good sequence [mq8qI2hag0I @ 00:13:51].

callout.title: Free-Service Leverage That Locks Plumbers In
callout.body: The operators who win plumbers treat free work and plumber education as entry tickets. They do not treat them as charity.
items: On a plumber-caused job, use the unbilled invoice to get past the front-desk gatekeeper and reach the decision-maker [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — ufmHlZ6tfKg @ 00:01:04].

Never charge a plumber for containment. Keep it under 90 minutes and build a doorway drying chamber, because charging a plumber a dime for anything is the trap [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — ufmHlZ6tfKg @ 00:02:04].

Label free dry-outs 'water – free dryout' on the job board, and run different protocols for them, such as top-down drying instead of hammers [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — ufmHlZ6tfKg @ 00:05:54].
Hand plumbers a Category 2 vs. Category 3 cheat sheet. If they don't know what to look for, they miss jobs that could easily have been yours [Marketing Ninjas — n7ECptsaJTQ @ 00:03:13].

sop_steps.action: Build a call list of residential service plumbers absent from Google's front page, then call them posing as a customer.

sop_steps.action: Deploy the matched incentive, such as the slow-leak card drip, free leads, or free dry-outs, and measure who sends work.
