sections.title: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split in the plumber channel is cash. Restorex Disaster Restoration runs a money-first program out of Indianapolis, advertising the highest referral fees in its market, paid as a percentage of the dry-out that ranges from a couple hundred to a couple thousand dollars, with payment landing the next day or when the job starts [nFvUl2Kjwjs @ 00:00:37]. Jon Schoen lists cash as the first lever, either a flat dollar amount or a percentage of the job, with the market deciding which [HFcU3Nls6fM @ 00:00:20]. Marketing Ninjas takes the opposite position: a $250 fee gets beaten by a $300 fee, kickbacks stay transactional and sketchy, and plumbers never brag about a $150 check, so the playbook replaces cash with a four-tier ladder of priority dispatch, free dry-outs, dumpsters, co-branded materials, raffles and team dinners [5Ibyq8oHR7Y @ 00:00:17]. Shane O'Dazier sits in the middle. Shane tells operators never to pay unless the plumber asks, because unsolicited money means you are no longer different, and warns that a rival will always pay ten or twenty more; when money is on the table, Shane incentivizes the tech and gives more to the GM or owner, while noting some plumbing companies ban tech fees outright [D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:10:16].

Free services split the field just as hard. Shane frames free dry-outs as the path to 500k of plumber referrals, labeling them "water - free dryout" on the job board, running different protocols such as top-down drying instead of hammers, and never charging a plumber for containment [ufmHlZ6tfKg @ 00:05:54]. Yet Shane also reports that free dry-outs, swag, referral fees, breakfasts and motorcycle giveaways all failed with the top plumber, and that the door only opened after roughly four months of servant marketing, when Shane ate a $300 mortar patch an hour away rather than marking it up to $600 [Rcmd8gVFzB8 @ 00:10:43]. Shane's guardrail is that free dry-outs need a 4:1 ratio of converted claims behind them [D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:12:00]. Jon Schoen runs a cheaper, event-driven playbook: a yearly bucket giveaway with one entry per referral for a used WaveRunner, four-wheeler or boat bought inexpensively, plus hot dog, burrito or chili lunches at Home Depot and Lowe's distributor counters, while warning those counters already rotate two or three restoration companies [HFcU3Nls6fM @ 00:02:43]. Shane's version is a slow, personal favor bank built one plumber at a time; Schoen's version is a cheap, repeatable circuit built around raffle entries and distributor-counter food that reaches many plumbers at once.

On the close, the phone camps diverge on what to say first. Restoration Made Simple teaches reading the caller, calm versus panicking, regular versus after-hours, and warns that pitching insurance to a self-pay caller loses them; its Strategy 11 promises arrival in under 60 minutes and a callback in three to five minutes so the homeowner waits instead of dialing a competitor [8nQyv3vEI6A @ 00:11:00]. Albi's framework is stricter: a scripted greeting, three qualifiers, no price ranges on the phone, no outsourced answering, and a target close rate of 75 to 80 percent, with anything under 70 percent signaling a missing system [mq8qI2hag0I @ 00:03:22]. Where Restoration Made Simple leans on local proof such as a shop fifteen minutes away and a tech in Littleton, Albi pushes a harder money ask on site: homeowner financing that makes the job cost incurred, or at minimum a deposit, plus 0% APR for 36 months when the insurance objection surfaces [mq8qI2hag0I @ 00:10:38]. claimhelpme rejects the common habit of taking the undisputed amount, starting, and supplementing later, telling contractors to review the carrier estimate immediately and ask the carrier to stop the check, because otherwise they are selling from weakness instead of knowledge [eLQHV7yIGx8 @ 00:00:39].

sections.title: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Shane's targeting trap is judging plumbers by truck count. A one-truck service plumber sees leaks, while a twenty-truck construction outfit only sends warranty jobs, so the target is service over construction and residential over commercial, where the property manager controls the referral and the contract has to be with the owner [D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:06:47]. Shane also says to avoid multi-family and commercial policies in the first few years. Guessing what a plumber wants flips a positive relationship negative fast, and triangulating questions catch liars, such as the plumber who claims to refer nobody but still wants a referral fee [D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:22:40]. The relationship can also turn on you after it lands. A referring plumber may fire you if you use another plumber, so Shane offers them the work with an "adjuster's only given me this amount" framing, while warning that retail plumbers who quoted $5,500 for half a day can charge $4,000 for a $600 task, which makes them the wrong hire for recon [MLuoMdYemWU @ 00:09:34]. Marketing Ninjas adds that plumbers see twelve rivals a month; in the extreme, one client brings a monkey into the plumbing offices, and the playbook adds branded shutoff tags and photo books [n7ECptsaJTQ @ 00:02:20].

The recon and big-loss traps hit cash flow. Shane warns that a $25K reconstruction job is tempting but ties you up six to fourteen weeks and puts the review at risk, and that on the internet side one "Yahoo" spending $25K a month wrecks the metrics that once delivered six jobs a week inside a 33-mile radius [xXe9Z763dDc @ 00:07:36]. Rowdy Legs of Homeway in Memphis reached $6.7M doing recon-only for one partner, and the split cost Homeway five to six jobs a week [Fj9S8rNJ5d4 @ 00:05:01]. Vinnie Mac's client Jim of Pride Restoration in St. Louis turned a Google Guarantee lead that cost a couple hundred dollars into a 70-unit, three-floor pipe burst worth more than $2M, but the payer moved from Farmers to the plumber's insurer to the owner's insurer with a PA involved [KYZjCfsaWhs @ 00:04:29]. Vinnie Mac's checks: hold cash reserves, file a preliminary notice of lien, partner with or refer to a larger firm when the job is too big, and remember a large loss can end in bankruptcy if you don't get paid [KYZjCfsaWhs @ 00:10:18]. Answering only 30 percent of calls, Vinnie Mac adds, burns the ad spend that produced the lead in the first place.

The closing failures are mostly unmeasured leaks. Restoration Made Simple sees clients spending $5k, $10k or $30k a month on marketing without tracking it, against lead costs of $300, $500 or $800 and as high as $1,500 to $1,600 in some regions; the fix is CallRail recording every call, a separate tracking number per site, call whispers like "plumbing referral 800 number," and source-level job averages that expose $3,000 versus $8,000 gaps [8nQyv3vEI6A @ 00:05:36]. Albi treats a close rate under 70 percent as a missing system and counts follow-up as recoverable revenue: follow up every 24 hours, and two of five leads that don't close initially later close with a good sequence; silence is part of the close [mq8qI2hag0I @ 00:13:51]. Shane frames the deeper failure as ownership: 99 percent of owners are weak at sales and marketing, an operator has about five years to figure it out, and franchises sell pipe dreams [sUMKhFYRGSQ @ 00:02:20]. Delegating too early backfires as well, because marketing hires fail 80 percent of the time, so Shane puts founder-first marketing ahead of hiring until the referral tree reaches at least three jobs within 90 days [xXe9Z763dDc @ 00:19:11].

callout.title: Four checks before money, free work, or a big loss goes out the door
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a trap a named practitioner hit or warned about firsthand.
items: Do not pay a plumber unless they ask, and only run free dry-outs where a 4:1 ratio of converted claims backs them up [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:12:00].
Never charge a plumber a dime for anything, including containment, which should stay under 90 minutes [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — ufmHlZ6tfKg @ 00:02:04].
Review the carrier estimate immediately and ask the carrier to stop the check before accepting the undisputed amount [claimhelpme — eLQHV7yIGx8 @ 00:00:39].

On a large loss, hold cash reserves and file a preliminary notice of lien, or partner with a larger firm if the job is too big [Water Damage Restoration Marketing - Vinnie Mac — KYZjCfsaWhs @ 00:09:49].

action_checklist: Call target plumbers as a customer, not a solicitor, run the water heater and pop-off valve script, and log each plumber's incentive preference and current fee tier (under $300, $300, $500, over $500) in the CRM [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:21:22].

Build the target list from residential service plumbers and shadow plumbers missing from Google's front page, not construction outfits judged by truck count [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — D4BavFC6d1E @ 00:16:59].
Launch a 30-day double-commission fast-start bonus and hand plumbers a Category 2 versus Category 3 cheat sheet [Marketing Ninjas — n7ECptsaJTQ @ 00:01:55].

Run the slow leak play: get the plumber on site, ask who the office calls, and hand over a card pre-loaded with $100 plus a $100 weekly drip, then judge fit after about 4 weeks [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — CV0x51fC7pw @ 00:02:34].
Give every source its own CallRail tracking number and call whisper, such as plumbing referral 800 number, and promise a callback in 3 to 5 minutes [Restoration Made Simple — 8nQyv3vEI6A @ 00:04:29].

On site, ask for a crew within the next 30 minutes, take financing or a deposit, and follow up every 24 hours on leads that do not close [Restoration Success Strategies | Albi — mq8qI2hag0I @ 00:09:48].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I start a restoration company, buy emergency leads online, structure contracts, and protect margins?
chapters.title: Launching the Restoration Company: Contracts, Paid Leads, and Margin
chapters.subtitle: Starting a water damage company without millions, how restoration differs from general contracting, work authorizations vs. reconstruction contracts, AOB vs. direction to pay, Google Local Services Ads and emergency search ads, the 2026 LSA changes, markup vs. margin, post-sale margin leaks, and a $14M-to-$55M scaling case
chapters.executive_summary: Restoration operators launching in 2026 converge on a narrow wedge: emergency water mitigation sold under a signed work authorization, fed by Google Local Services Ads and controlled PPC, and priced off margin rather than markup. Albi pegs startup purchasing power at $50-200K and mitigation gross margins above 70%, pushing rebuilds to a GC for a 10% kickback until $3-5M. Vinnie Mac reports LSA leads at $400-500 in CA, FL, NY and TX versus $120-220 in IL, MO, OK and LA, with the August 2026 migration into Performance Max wiping visibility history. Shane O'Dazier builds paper around 20% termination fees and three-day equipment minimums, while Florida counsel Hans Kennan steers toward direction-to-pay after the AOB ban. Splits remain on service-area width, the keyword 'cheap', AOB use, and whether Xactimate and dry logs matter at launch.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every launch playbook starts narrow. Albi of Restoration Success Strategies tells new owners to run emergency water mitigation only, a line carrying 70%+ gross margins, and to refer rebuilds to a general contractor for a 10% kickback until revenue clears $3-5M, summed up as "Simple scales and complex fails" [3PlUwHvZkxE @ 00:02:56]. PushLeads' Jeremy draws the same line from the customer side: mitigation and reconstruction are sequential phases, not rival bids, and "The restoration company always comes first," because mold can take hold within 24-48 hours and the carrier may then deny the mold claim [wnVxHv3JM28 @ 00:01:01]. The money sits in that first phase. Albi's second guide puts the average restoration ticket at $8-12K against $2-3K for a plumbing call, with drying equipment running and billed on site for five to seven days [MDZLPIkMaI8 @ 00:03:58]. Capital requirements are modest by contracting standards. Albi wants $50-200K of purchasing power counting loans, plus one referral source, while Restoration Made Simple, built on 18 years and two from-scratch companies, quotes $50-100K typical and $10-30K for bootstrappers, with the first $1-2K going to WRT and ASD certification taken together at a flood house [aBQA1Wn_LNQ @ 00:01:42]. Both treat the 24/7 phone as the real job description, and Restoration Made Simple warns the business never closes.

The second consensus point: own the phone. Albi credits half of Mason Dixon Restoration's $2.6M first nine months to online marketing and names Google LSA, Google PPC and a lead aggregator as the stack that takes a shop from $0 to $1M, with plumbers preferred over insurance agents as the second source [3PlUwHvZkxE @ 00:07:50]. Vinnie Mac, who runs dozens of LSA campaigns, explains why Google wins: roughly 90-95% of search goes there, the LSA unit sits at the top of the page, review stars trigger an "Amazon effect," and only qualified phone calls count, not clicks or impressions [IDqwheOOgb0 @ 00:09:52]. In a later breakdown, the agency reports "about 80% of the phone calls come from either Google Guaranteed or Google Maps," and that lead-gen outfits such as 33 Mile Radius and Inquirly cannot qualify for the placement [O0STLVhCL2c @ 00:08:54]. The 2026 update adds a warning that LSA does not stand alone: results track Maps, SEO and PPC visibility, and "You can't just turn on LSA" [2akNGTmJry8 @ 00:03:48]. The ad operators all land on the same rule for what happens after the ring: pick up live, around the clock, with no voicemail. Restoration Made Simple puts the conversion side bluntly: "Doesn't do us any good to get the phone to ring if we can't convert them."

On paper, contract specialists who otherwise fight over details agree on one sequence: signature before work. Shane O'Dazier of RestorationProfits wants a reconstruction "agreement," named that way to kill the "not a contract" defense, signed before any estimate is written, with no free estimates ever, plus a separate work authorization for tarping, mitigation, mold, asbestos and bio, and both signed when in doubt [b1-Dcqk4F9g @ 00:01:57]. C&R Magazine's guest Ed, "the Restoration Lawyer," states the same priority: "We want to make sure we have a signature first from somebody who is financially responsible in agreeing to pay," preferring fixed-price over time-and-materials [t7tJ735gl4s @ 00:03:31]. Florida counsel Hans Kennan, on Contractor Talk Podcast with Richie Kidwell, recommends a service authorization with direction to pay on 90-day net terms and rejects contingency contracts [Tg526FvHOmY @ 00:27:01]. Margin is the final shared prerequisite. George Gabriel warns that on insurance work the carrier sets the price, so cost is the only lever: "So you can't fix a thin job by putting more markup on it" [KnWhJDOPsTc @ 00:04:04]. Albi's homeowner rule closes the loop: the homeowner, not the carrier, owes the bill, so collect the $2-3K deductible up front and let the insurance check on the back end become the profit.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Albi's launch budget runs about $200K, half cash and half financed. A new Sprinter van costs roughly $60K plus a $6,500 wrap, about $800 a month financed; $45K of equipment financed at 8-10% buys 8 dehus, 80 air movers, one extractor and four scrubbers; then $5K a year in insurance, $1K legal, $12K for office and warehouse, $10-20K for web and marketing, and a 60-90 day cash cushion [3PlUwHvZkxE @ 00:05:22]. Ram Exterior proved the floor is lower, starting on $30K of Menards and Chase Ink credit plus a truck. Staffing stays at three roles, crew chief, technician and executive assistant, and growth comes from adding trucks rather than middle managers: "a two-person unit can produce a million dollars of revenue per year, $83,000 per month" [3PlUwHvZkxE @ 00:07:09]. Restoration Made Simple adds the closing kit: an infrared camera at about $500-800 or a phone plug-in, a moisture meter and a hydro sensor, worked as a "double visual close" on the claim that 65% of people react to visuals; one extra closed job pays for all three [aBQA1Wn_LNQ @ 00:03:20]. On the phone, the script asks "what city do you live in?" and holds the full address until the job is sold [aBQA1Wn_LNQ @ 00:06:44].

The paper carries specific numbers. Shane O'Dazier sells "5 000 worth of agreements for under 50 bucks," built around a Clause 6 that bills any portion of a day as a full 24 hours with a three-day minimum on equipment rental, which strips the adjuster's main argument even though the check still has to be collected [b1-Dcqk4F9g @ 00:06:15]. The termination clause charges the customer 20% of the gross job if they fire the contractor after the estimate and negotiation; O'Dazier dismisses public-adjuster and legality objections, keeps an AOB-style right to endorse and deposit the check even where a state voids it, adds an attorney-fee provision, and calls California's roughly 10% deposit limit "stupid" and something to violate [b1-Dcqk4F9g @ 00:10:02]. Ed's CAT-work method phases emergency work into a fixed-price contract: price the first 24-48 hours, such as "half a dozen air movers and D U and and 10 labor hours," promise nothing about pre-loss condition, then follow up with a change order [t7tJ735gl4s @ 00:03:48]. Against mortgage companies, Ed sends a photocopy of the check plus a contract obligating them to endorse and return it, and pairs an assignment with a direction to pay so the contractor's name lands on the check [t7tJ735gl4s @ 00:07:14].

Paid-lead setup is equally specific. Vinnie Mac sets the LSA budget above intended spend, up to "99,999" a week, because franchises outbid smaller shops, notes that overnight calls cost more but are more profitable, and recommends $1,500-$2,000 a week: "I would not start out at $250 per week" [IDqwheOOgb0 @ 00:25:33]. Launch on automated bidding, move to target cost per lead after 30-60 days, ignore Google's leads-per-week projection ("This is false"), answer message leads inside 30-60 minutes, and qualify callers within 60-90 seconds [O0STLVhCL2c @ 00:16:02]. On PPC, Restoration Growth Co shows the leak: four clicks at $34 each for one booked job is $136 per job, and the fix is shutting off broad match, search partners, display expansion and "presence or interest" location targeting, then adding campaign-level phrase negatives like salary, jobs, DIY, how to, certification and rental [zkR_04H9hBQ @ 00:06:07]. PushLeads prices emergency clicks at $50-100 against $3-15K jobs, so the account runs exact match, phrase at most, never broad, with urgency modifiers like emergency, 24-7, near me, same day and after hours, CallRail counting calls over 1-2 minutes as conversions, and bids raised on nights and weekends [9FnufX3pXj4 @ 00:03:23].

callout.title: Small settings that move lead cost and close rate
callout.body: Four low-effort adjustments the paid-lead operators run on live restoration accounts.
items: Mark every qualified LSA lead as booked even when the job is lost, because "even if you didn't win the job market is booked because it was a qualified that call call that came in" [Water Damage Restoration Marketing - Vinnie Mac — IDqwheOOgb0 @ 00:30:42].

Never pause an LSA campaign to save money; drop the budget to something like $30 instead, since stopping and restarting acts as a reset [Water Damage Restoration Marketing - Vinnie Mac — O0STLVhCL2c @ 00:41:54].

sop_steps.title: Paper the job before the first air mover
sop_steps.action: Get the work authorization and reconstruction agreement signed, then price the first 24-48 hours as a fixed-price phase.
sop_steps.detail: Have the customer sign the work authorization for emergency work and the reconstruction agreement before any estimate, signing both when in doubt [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — b1-Dcqk4F9g @ 00:03:50]; scope the first 24-48 hours at a fixed price and handle the rest by change order [C&R Magazine — t7tJ735gl4s @ 00:03:48].

sop_steps.title: Clear LSA verification and launch the budget
sop_steps.action: Load the $1M liability COI, the IICRC firm certification with an exact name match, and at least 3 Google reviews.
sop_steps.detail: Verification checks the owner's background, a certificate of insurance showing $1M liability, an IICRC firm certification costing a few hundred dollars with the name matching exactly, and a profile with at least 3 reviews [Water Damage Restoration Marketing - Vinnie Mac — O0STLVhCL2c @ 00:11:50].

sop_steps.title: Lock down PPC intent every Monday
sop_steps.action: Switch location targeting to presence, kill broad match, and read the search terms report weekly.
sop_steps.detail: Every Monday spend 20 minutes on the last 90 days of search terms sorted by cost, reading the top 50 rows and adding phrase-match negatives at campaign level [Restoration Growth Co — zkR_04H9hBQ @ 00:08:37].

sop_steps.title: Price off margin and write the phase budget
sop_steps.action: Convert the target margin into markup, then write a phase-by-phase budget that sums to the contract price.
sop_steps.detail: A 30% margin requires a 43% markup, or $3,440 on an $8,000 job [Roofing Insights — ppn4akh1gPo @ 00:02:55]; at signing, write a phase-by-phase budget that sums exactly to the contract price and classify every overrun as your miss or a change order [George Gabriel — KnWhJDOPsTc @ 00:02:53].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Contract philosophy splits between an aggressive paper camp and a cautious lawyer camp. Shane O'Dazier tells operators to title the document an 'agreement' to kill the 'not a contract' defense, sign it before writing any estimate, and keep the AOB clause even where a state voids it, because it works like a limited power of attorney to endorse and deposit the check [b1-Dcqk4F9g @ 00:08:02]. He stacks a termination clause billing 20% of the gross job if the homeowner fires the contractor after estimate and negotiation, dismisses PA and legality objections, and says he would violate California's roughly 10% deposit limit because it is 'stupid' [b1-Dcqk4F9g @ 00:10:02]. Ed, the Restoration Lawyer on C&R Magazine, runs the opposite play: phase emergency work into a fixed-price contract covering the first 24 to 48 hours, commit to nothing about pre-loss condition, follow up with a change order, and 'think twice' before using assignments in Florida after the insurer lobby passed its counter-law [t7tJ735gl4s @ 00:10:25]. Hans Kennan on Contractor Talk Podcast lands in the middle: with the Florida AOB ban hitting policies issued or renewed from 2023 onward, he pushes a service authorization with direction to pay on 90-day net terms and rejects contingency contracts [Tg526FvHOmY @ 00:27:01].

The billing stack splits just as hard. Albi of Restoration Success Strategies calls mandatory Xactimate a myth, pointing to Rhino Restoration reaching $3M on 95% retail work, and reports that 300+ attendees at the RAA conference said documentation did not speed payment, with his own data suggesting about 70% of dry logs are 'not real.' He adds that TPAs control only 10 to 15% of dollar volume, demand 2 years of history, and route work to top contractors by algorithm [3PlUwHvZkxE @ 00:09:35]. Restoration Made Simple bets the other way on paper: room-by-room Excel sheets catch missed line items on every job, and a dedicated self-pay sheet helped crews in Colorado and Utah close 3 to 5 more self-pay jobs a month [aBQA1Wn_LNQ @ 00:05:33]. Payment timing is the sharpest contrast. Albi insists the homeowner, not the carrier, owes the bill, so the $2,000 to $3,000 deductible gets collected up front: 'that cash covers the payroll for the job, and the insurance check on the back end is just the profit' [3PlUwHvZkxE @ 00:14:12]. Kennan, speaking to homeowners on Contractor Talk Podcast, gives the opposite instruction: never pay up front, verify license and insurance, and lean toward big names such as SERVPRO [Tg526FvHOmY @ 00:36:52]. Albi treats the deductible as the payroll engine; Kennan treats an up-front ask as the red flag.

Even inside one agency, the Google playbook shifts year to year. Vinnie Mac's 2024 LSA session says 'go wider than narrow' on service areas, pushing a south Chicago account into Indiana for fringe opportunities [IDqwheOOgb0 @ 00:27:59]. The 2026 version narrows that advice: use cities and zip codes instead of counties when results are weak, and stop pushing outward because the account loses to competitors closer to the searcher [2akNGTmJry8 @ 00:25:28]. That same 2026 session flips credentials and budgets too, moving from a firm-level IICRC certification to a state-by-state IICRC or contractor license requirement, and from weekly to daily budgets under the Performance Max migration. On paid search, Restoration Growth Co tells operators to keep 'cost' and 'cheap' live, calling that 'the best term in your whole account,' and to route technician searches to a careers page through a separate $5/day campaign rather than only blocking them [zkR_04H9hBQ @ 00:07:41]. PushLeads preloads 'cheap' and 'free' as negatives alongside job, salary, DIY, and out-of-area cities, runs exact match with phrase at most, never broad, and reviews the negative list weekly because every click in this vertical costs $50 to $100 [9FnufX3pXj4 @ 00:04:03].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Lead spend bleeds before a truck ever rolls. Restoration Growth Co breaks down one booked job from four $34 clicks, a true $136 per job, where the other three clicks were a technician hunting 'jobs,' a DIY 'how to' searcher, and a landlord 200 miles away; the fix is not cheaper CPC but shutting off broad match, search partners, display expansion, and 'presence or interest' location targeting [zkR_04H9hBQ @ 00:00:26]. PushLeads raises the stakes with $50 to $100 clicks and warns that 'no one is filling out a form,' so the phone has to be staffed live 24/7 with bids raised on nights and weekends [9FnufX3pXj4 @ 00:04:23]. On LSA, Vinnie Mac calls Google's weekly lead projections 'false' peak numbers and notes dispute credits land 30 to 45 days later as next-month offsets, not card refunds [IDqwheOOgb0 @ 00:16:40]. The 2026 session lists the self-inflicted wounds: starting and stopping a campaign acts as a reset, one or two missed calls kill a profile, expired documents knock the account offline, unresolved Google Business Profile suspensions linger, and Google still charges when the operator refers a caller to another company [2akNGTmJry8 @ 00:36:16]. The cure he teaches is lowering hours, bid, or territory instead of pausing outright.

Margin dies twice, once in the pricing math and again in the field. Roofing Insights shows a $10,000 price on $8,000 cost is a 20% margin but a 25% markup, and blames contractors 'thinking in dollars and not percentages'; hitting 30% on that $8,000 job takes a 43% markup, or $3,440 [ppn4akh1gPo @ 00:01:58]. George Gabriel walks one job where a second dumpster haul ($450), two bundles short ($180), and a second shingle layer at 25 squares times $25 ($625) stacked into a $1,255 overrun that dropped margin from 33% to 25%, against a net profit band of only 6 to 12% [KnWhJDOPsTc @ 00:02:03]. His insurance-work warning is blunt: the carrier sets the price, so 'you can't fix a thin job by putting more markup on it,' and cost is the only lever; his fix is a phase-by-phase budget written at signing that sums exactly to the contract price, with every overrun classed as either the contractor's miss or a change order [KnWhJDOPsTc @ 00:04:04]. On the Roofing Insights growth panel, Alex describes a 7pm 'money in/money out' report that flags every job under 35% margin in red, replacing the 4 to 6 month margin lag of after-the-fact accounting [evwV66xRf4I @ 00:47:08].

Collections is where unsigned paper and slow timelines cost real money. Shane O'Dazier warns that without a signed agreement before the estimate, the homeowner gets the check and stops returning calls, a trap he ties directly to re-roofs, and he refuses to give free estimates at all [b1-Dcqk4F9g @ 00:03:24]. His 3-day minimum rental clause, counting any portion of a day as a full 24 hours, strips the adjuster's argument but still does not guarantee payment [b1-Dcqk4F9g @ 00:07:36]. In Florida, Kennan lays out the squeeze: insurers now pay or deny within 60 days instead of 90, contractors hold a 90-day lien window, and that leaves roughly 30 days to appraise, mediate, or litigate [Tg526FvHOmY @ 00:41:11]. Ed adds the mortgage-company trap, protecting against it by sending a photocopy of the check plus a contract obligating the lender to endorse and return it, and recounts forcing carriers to pay a second time 'because the policyholder ran off to Hawaii with the money or used the money to pay off the mortgage' [t7tJ735gl4s @ 00:16:05]. His escalation rule is not too fast and not too slow, because older debts are harder to collect, and never experiment with mechanics liens because the deadlines are strict.

callout.title: Four Gates Before Spending on Leads or Rolling Equipment
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, reversal, or bottleneck a practitioner hit firsthand. Clear all four before scaling ad spend or adding trucks.
items: Paper gate: the signed agreement is in hand before any estimate is written, with no free estimates, so the homeowner cannot take the check and go silent [Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits — b1-Dcqk4F9g @ 00:02:15].

Timeline gate: on Florida claims, map the 60-day pay-or-deny clock against the 90-day lien window so the roughly 30 days left for appraisal, mediation, or litigation are not burned [Contractor Talk Podcast — Tg526FvHOmY @ 00:19:47].

Phone gate: every LSA call is answered live with no voicemail or AI answering service, because one or two missed calls kill a profile [Water Damage Restoration Marketing - Vinnie Mac — 2akNGTmJry8 @ 00:35:15].
Margin gate: every job carries a written landing budget before work starts, because a job sliding cannot be caught without one [George Gabriel — KnWhJDOPsTc @ 00:02:28].

chapters.pull_quote: 'You can't catch a job sliding if you never wrote down where it was supposed to land.' — George Gabriel (KnWhJDOPsTc @ 00:02:28).
action_checklist: Line up $50K to $200K of purchasing power including loans, then put about $45K into 8 dehus, 80 air movers, 1 extractor, and 4 scrubbers at 8 to 10%, keeping a 60 to 90 day cash cushion [Restoration Success Strategies | Albi — 3PlUwHvZkxE @ 00:05:22].
Spend the first $1,000 to $2,000 on education and take WRT and ASD together with hands-on work at a flood house [Restoration Made Simple — aBQA1Wn_LNQ @ 00:02:10].

Clear LSA verification: owner background check, a Certificate of Insurance showing $1M liability, an IICRC firm certification whose name matches Google exactly, and at least 3 reviews [Water Damage Restoration Marketing - Vinnie Mac — O0STLVhCL2c @ 00:11:50].

Put a tracking number with a 'Google Local Service' whisper on the profile and qualify every caller on issue, location, homeowner status, decision-maker, and insurance [Water Damage Restoration Marketing - Vinnie Mac — 2akNGTmJry8 @ 00:28:42].

Every Monday, pull the search terms report for the last 90 days, sort by cost, read the top 50 rows, and add phrase-match negatives at the campaign level [Restoration Growth Co — zkR_04H9hBQ @ 00:08:37].
Get a signature first from the party responsible for paying, price the first 24 to 48 hours as a fixed-price phase, and follow up with a change order [C&R Magazine — t7tJ735gl4s @ 00:03:31].

chapters.question_prompt: What is an assignment of benefits, when does it work for contractors, and why did Florida move to restrict it?
chapters.title: Assignment of Benefits: Mechanics, Abuse, and Reform
chapters.subtitle: How AOBs transfer claim control, when AOB works best for emergency-service restorers, signing at the front door, homeowner AOB experiences, Florida insurer reform push, lawmakers' proposed bans, the Florida property insurance crisis, and Medicare/medical AOB billing parallels
chapters.executive_summary: Restoration operators, public adjusters, and Florida reform voices agree on what an assignment of benefits does: it moves the right to be paid, and the right to sue, from the homeowner to the contractor. Josh Ehmke and Steve Dunn treat it as receivables armor that ends owners spending carrier checks and contractors suing their own customers. The street mechanics run on split claims, with emergency mitigation under the assignment and reconstruction upgrades on change orders, plus 10-page iPad work orders, powers of attorney, and loss-draft delays stretching months. The abuse side runs on numbers: an $8,000 estimate billed at $22,000, $1,000 to $2,000 plumber kickbacks, a 6,800 percent jump in suits, and the one-dollar fee trigger. The split: Ehmke says anti-AOB states hurt policyholders, while Florida officials want the tool limited or banned.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: An assignment of benefits transfers the homeowner's right to the insurance claim to a third party, usually a contractor, roofer, or restoration company, and every property-side speaker describes the same handoff. The Fine Print lays it out bluntly: once signed, the contractor steps into the homeowner's shoes, negotiates with the insurer, submits the invoices, decides what the repair costs, and gains the right to sue the carrier using the homeowner's policy [UxKcyrt-VS0 @ 00:00:31]. Happy Adjuster adds that the assignee can file paperwork and even receive payment without needing the homeowner's approval [hqbiodyd1gc @ 00:00:00]. Corey Locke and Troy Willis sharpen the line operators actually work inside: the policy itself is never assigned, and the anti-assignment clause in every policy is not what it appears to be. What moves is the financial piece already performed, the right to be paid for that portion of the loss [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:04:28]. Steve Dunn, working the long-term care side in Florida, frames the payoff for the provider: the assignment lets the entity stand in the shoes of the insured with the same rights and benefits under the policy, which turns a soft receivable into an enforceable claim against the carrier rather than a collection problem with the customer [4AHP633shFk @ 00:02:25].

The core business reason is cash protection, and the speakers who build collection operations agree on it. Josh Ehmke of One Claim Solution came out of medical billing and ported the hospital model into restoration around 2014 and 2015, because the check that lands with the policyholder tends to arrive right when the truck breaks or the family vacation is overdue, and then the contractor hears 'tough luck, I can make payments, or you can try to come after me' [wq1z-Qyyws8 @ 00:01:33]. Jeremy Traasdahl adds that even honest owners misread an ambiguous carrier check and spend the mitigation money upgrading countertops [wq1z-Qyyws8 @ 00:02:25]. Steve Dunn makes the same case from the agency side: without the assignment, the only recourse is suing your own clients, often elderly people with no money, sometimes waiting on an estate, and paying your own lawyer to do it [4AHP633shFk @ 00:03:05]. Locke and Willis confirm why mitigators insist on it: nobody wants to put crews and costs on a loss without a security interest, and some carriers now accept the assignment specifically for mitigation because that work is finished before payment and the mortgage company has no stake in it [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:05:30].

Where the speakers converge on the downside, they describe one engine: fee-shifting. The Fine Print explains that Florida law for years awarded attorney fees to whoever held the claim, so a contractor winning even a small disputed amount could recover large legal fees, and the lawsuit itself became the business model, with AOB suits climbing from a few thousand a year to tens of thousands over the 2010s [UxKcyrt-VS0 @ 00:01:55]. yourEadvisor.com walks the same math on a roof: if the result lands even $1 over the insurer's number, the insurer owes the contractor's fees [On3xbq5nLqk @ 00:02:01]. The fix also converges. The speaker on Floridians For Honest Lending argues assignments should be limited to emergency service work, such as a middle-of-the-night dry-out costing $1,000 or $2,000 the homeowner cannot front, while kitchen and roof replacements needing pricing, permits, and inspections months out require no doorstep signature [I-S4L6YL2wo @ 00:03:46]. Josh Ehmke's own operation reflects that line in practice: OCS works only with emergency services contractors and does not take reconstruction contractors, because the emergency side is where the tool fits best [F4WLuIxWd-Q @ 00:05:15].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Josh Ehmke's working model starts by splitting every claim in two. The emergency bucket covers water mitigation, mold remediation, and contents, which are rarely agreed up front because true extent and saturation stay unknown until materials get pulled apart, so that open-ended scope is exactly what the assignment handles cleanly. The reconstruction bucket gets an estimate agreed with the carrier before a hammer swings, and any owner upgrade above the approved scope, like the cabinets they have been meaning to replace, moves to a separate change order outside the assignment [F4WLuIxWd-Q @ 00:02:56]. When OCS onboards a contractor, it reviews paperwork and past invoices against state requirements, leaning on thousands of claims processed every month to see how carriers like submissions packaged, and points out liabilities contractors are leaving themselves open to; the rule is the more documentation the better. The firm says it has never written an invoice, chases only charges the documentation supports, and plays liaison when an adjuster will approve a line once a missing piece arrives [F4WLuIxWd-Q @ 00:08:46]. Kim Phillips of Tyro Health flags the same friction from medical billing: when the assignment is captured outside the claim submission flow, practices eat extra authorization steps, follow-ups, payment delays, and front-desk workload [CbZ5Nrxx8Xw @ 00:01:42].

On the mitigation floor, the assignment rarely appears as a standalone form. Corey Locke describes the mitigator walking on with an iPad and a work order roughly 10 pages long, sign here, initial here, date here, with the assignment buried in the boilerplate, so ServiceMaster, Servpro, or Rainbow crews get paid directly for tear-out, flood cuts, and dry-down, sometimes on a check that also lists the insured but leaves out the mortgage company [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:06:41]. Troy Willis explains why every East Coast mitigation contract in their experience carried a power of attorney: loss draft departments take a month or two to release funds, the contractor's bank then puts a 15 to 20 day hold on a couple hundred thousand dollars, and the insurer may already have taken three or four months [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:17:11]. The same contracts now stack mechanics liens and five-day payment demands, in an industry where Willis says nothing happens in five days [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:27:04]. On the acquisition side, Floridians For Honest Lending documents restoration contractors paying plumbers $1,000 or $2,000 cash per water-damage referral, undisclosed to the homeowner, against a plumber wage of $500 to $600 a week, turning the plumber into a solicitor [I-S4L6YL2wo @ 00:02:18].

The dispute economics run on a simple spread. yourEadvisor.com walks the sequence from a door-knock on a roof that 'could have been from hail' to a signature, then an inflated claim, then an insurer counter built in the estimating system all adjusters use plus an extra ten percent for expenses that pop up. From there the fight moves to arbitration or court in what the speaker calls a very litigious state: with the contractor at $50,000 and the carrier at $25,000, landing even $1 over the carrier's figure puts the contractor's court fees on the insurer, and any excess paid stays with the contractor rather than the insured [On3xbq5nLqk @ 00:01:44]. Jeff Grant of Bone-Dry Restoration and Cleaning argues the other side of that spread, saying nearly every insurer lowballs and will 'try to save 50 bucks' by doing the wrong thing, while the assignment recovers full costs and keeps repairs up to standard [7-KaOK5zk7g @ 00:01:09]. The rules then moved. The Fine Print cites House Bill 7065 in 2019 reshaping fees, mandating form disclosures, and adding a rescission window [UxKcyrt-VS0 @ 00:03:52], and Floridians For Honest Lending describes a 2020 sliding-scale proportional fee framework replacing the one-dollar trigger [I-S4L6YL2wo @ 00:06:29].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Josh Ehmke of One Claim Solution treats the assignment as a contractor's strongest payment shield: once the carrier has notice of the assignment and still mails the check to the homeowner, it stays obligated to cut a fresh check to the assignee and recover its own money from the policyholder, and legally it has to do it [F4WLuIxWd-Q @ 00:14:57]. Florida CFO Jimmy Patronis takes the opposite line on FOX 4, saying AOBs have to go because a homeowner assigning benefits to a person met at the doorstep hands over a blank check with access to the claim, even after the 2019 reform that required insurers to submit annual reports to the state but stopped short of an outright ban [Mzby_5C7IBI @ 00:00:47]. Troy Willis of Claims Underground lands in the middle. As a working contractor, Willis used assignments to make sure the money came back and still sees them as leverage for whoever does the job to get paid what they are entitled to, as long as nobody abuses the process [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:03:54]. But Willis also warns that a contractor carries no fiduciary responsibility to the homeowner the way a state-licensed public adjuster does, comparing it to handing your checkbook to the gym teacher instead of an accountant [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:02:47].

The second split is how far an assignment should reach. Ehmke's playbook carves every claim in two: emergency services such as water mitigation, mold remediation and contents run under the assignment because the true extent of saturation is never known until materials get pulled apart, while reconstruction runs on an estimate agreed with the carrier before a hammer swings, with any homeowner upgrade booked as a separate change order [F4WLuIxWd-Q @ 00:02:56]. OCS itself works only with emergency services contractors and has not found a need on the reconstruction side, though the team has looked at it [F4WLuIxWd-Q @ 00:04:56]. Floridians For Honest Lending wants that line written into law, limiting assignments to emergency work such as a middle-of-the-night dry-out costing $1,000 or $2,000 the homeowner may not have on hand, because a roof or kitchen replacement will not start for months while costs, permits and inspections get sorted, so nobody needs to assign benefits on the spot [I-S4L6YL2wo @ 00:04:54]. Claims Underground backs the mitigation carve-out from the adjusting side: some carriers now accept an assignment for mitigation because the work is finished by the time it is paid, the mortgage company has no stake in it, and putting the lender on that check only delays the mitigator [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:05:47].

Fee shifting is where the camps collide hardest, because it decides who funds the fight. Steve Dunn of the Long Term Care Law Office says the assignment lets home care agencies and registries stand in the insured's shoes, go after the carrier directly on short pays, and collect their attorney fees from the insurer when they prevail, instead of suing elderly clients and paying their own lawyers [4AHP633shFk @ 00:04:03]. With assignments in hand, Dunn's clients recovered in excess of a million dollars in receivables they had written off as uncollectible, at a very high collection rate and very low fee exposure [4AHP633shFk @ 00:04:46]. The reform proposal aired on News4JAX keeps fee protection for homeowners fighting their own insurers but strips the one-way attorney fee statute from any third party taking an assignment, placing the potential responsibility for paying legal fees on the contractors [hB0EZGfpw4I @ 00:01:20]. Floridians For Honest Lending defends fee shifting as a consumer protection, pointing out that a homeowner owed $15,000 who spends $20,000-plus on lawyers would walk away with nothing, then describes the 2020 law that replaced prevailing by a single dollar with a proportional sliding scale where recoverable fees track the percentage of indemnity won [I-S4L6YL2wo @ 00:06:10].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The Fine Print walks one porch signature to its end state. A first estimate of around $8,000 came back as a $22,000 invoice carrying water mitigation the homeowner did not remember and material quantities that did not match the roof, and when the insurer pushed back, the contractor sued in the policy's name for the disputed amount plus attorney fees [UxKcyrt-VS0 @ 00:01:05]. That lawsuit then sat on the homeowner's claims history, the carrier declined to renew, the next insurer saw a contested claim, and unwinding a 30-second signature took months and legal fees because the contractor had already started work and incurred costs [UxKcyrt-VS0 @ 00:03:02]. Tampa Bay 28 logged the same pattern on the remodeling side: in Davenport, Darlene Masters filed a claim for a small amount of water damage and says the contractor gutted the kitchen and took off, while in Pinellas County Wendy Snelgrove lost the use of a kitchen for more than a year after approving an assignment [1DrEImX-sYU @ 00:00:18]. After the station exposed contractors and attorneys inflating claims and then suing carriers, one homeowner put it bluntly: I sued somebody that I had no idea that I was suing. Citizens even admitted raising rates on its customers to offset the cost of these cases [1DrEImX-sYU @ 00:01:22].

Claims Underground traces the damage to the signing stack itself. The mitigator walks on with an iPad and a 10-page work order of sign here, initial here, date here boilerplate with the assignment buried inside, and the family signs while worried about where the kids go and the dog splashing through water [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:06:41]. Troy Willis reports customers saying the tech just scrolled to the next signature spot, then later facing $80,000 to $100,000 bills they never remember seeing, with charges as far-fetched as cleaning the boxes the crew brought to the house [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:14:12]. Willis also flags contracts that now slip mechanics liens in at the beginning, effectively warning the homeowner the lien goes on the house if the contractor does not get paid, and many of those contracts demand payment in five days when, after three decades in the industry, Willis has seen nothing happen in five days [bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:26:49]. Happy Adjuster warns that some contractors use the signed stack to take control of the claim and bill for work that is overpriced, unnecessary or never completed, after which the homeowner can be cut out of the conversation entirely and land in the middle of a legal dispute between the contractor and the insurer [hqbiodyd1gc @ 00:00:32].

The cash traps cut both directions. Barbara Day of AARP Florida reports that contractors wanted 50 percent down on a roof from the homeowner's insurance money, and chapter members who turned those funds over lost some of their money [vscXMMen_rc @ 00:01:54]. Floridians For Honest Lending exposes the referral economy behind the AOB boom: restoration contractors paid plumbers $1,000 to $2,000 cash per water-loss referral, turning a tradesman making five or six hundred dollars a week into an undisclosed solicitor whose homeowners believed they were getting the best qualified company [I-S4L6YL2wo @ 00:02:36]. On the contractor side, Josh Ehmke of One Claim Solution describes the insurance check that lands right when the policyholder's truck breaks or the family needs a vacation; the money gets spent, and the homeowner tells the contractor tough luck, make payments or come after me, I have nothing [wq1z-Qyyws8 @ 00:01:52]. yourEadvisor.com runs the insurer's math: a contractor bills $50,000 on a roof the carrier prices at $25,000, and if the split lands even $1 above the carrier's number, the insurer suddenly owes the contractor's court fees on top of the claim, which is how a basic roof replacement spirals into something far bigger than intended [On3xbq5nLqk @ 00:02:21].

callout.title: Kill the Deal Before the Signature If Any of These Hit
callout.body: Every item below traces to a loss a practitioner watched happen on a live claim.
items: Refuse any assignment, power of attorney or work order the company will not send by email or hard copy before the crew arrives; if they cannot give it to you before they show up, find another company [Claims Underground Podcast — bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:22:34].

Do not sign at the door: call your insurer, report the damage yourself and get your own written estimate first, because an $8,000 estimate became a $22,000 invoice and a lawsuit [The Fine Print — UxKcyrt-VS0 @ 00:04:09].
Walk away from any roofer demanding 50 percent down out of insurance proceeds; chapter members lost money doing exactly that [AARP Florida - The Sunshine State! — vscXMMen_rc @ 00:01:54].
Restorers: confirm the loss is covered before banking on the assignment, because a correct denial leaves no insurance rights to assign [magicplan — F4WLuIxWd-Q @ 00:14:03].

action_checklist: Before any contractor signature, call your insurer to report the damage yourself and get your own written estimate; never sign anything at the door [The Fine Print — UxKcyrt-VS0 @ 00:04:09].

Require the AOB, work order and any power of attorney by email or hard copy before the crew arrives, and replace any company that says it cannot send the form [Claims Underground Podcast — bPBmUaKay2w @ 00:22:34].

Restorers: split each claim into emergency services under the assignment and reconstruction on an estimate agreed with the carrier before a hammer swings, with upgrades on separate change orders [magicplan — F4WLuIxWd-Q @ 00:03:49].
Restorers: when a carrier pays the homeowner after notice of the assignment, go back to the carrier and demand a new check [magicplan — F4WLuIxWd-Q @ 00:15:32].

chapters.question_prompt: How do deductibles, insurance check endorsements, subrogation, and AOB litigation affect how contractors get paid?
chapters.title: Deductibles, Claim Checks, and Claim Law
chapters.subtitle: Why waiving deductibles is fraud, legally covering the deductible, explaining deductibles to insureds, deductible math, mortgage company check endorsement, subrogation and deductible refunds, salvage and fair claims practices, AOB claim litigation, and consumer warnings on AOB contractors
chapters.executive_summary: Restoration practitioners agree the deductible is withheld from the insurer's payout and handed by the homeowner to the contractor, and that a roofer who 'waives' or 'eats' it is usually inflating the estimate or cutting roof quality. Percentage deductibles blindside owners: 2% on a $500,000 dwelling is $10,000, and wind/hail riders can reach 5%. Mortgage-named checks run through a loss draft department demanding W-9s, lien waivers, contracts and inspections, with one lender releasing claims under $10,000 without holds. Chad Michael teaches legal deductible coverage by mining ACV-only other-structures money or subcontracting trades back to the owner, while calling invoice-lying a felony. Disagreement centers on assignment of benefits: Florida law honors post-loss AOBs, but carriers, public adjusters and regulators tie them to $40,000 water claims, liens and lawsuits.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who touched the money flow lands on the same mechanic: the insurer never bills the deductible, it subtracts it. Anne Pullen tells homeowners the deductible is money the carrier holds back from the payout, so in real life the owner is the one handing that cash to the contractor [tLwSSUZ6Awc @ 00:00:34]. Brent Simmons of Restoration Roofing runs a $20,000 roof with a $2,000 deductible: the carrier pays $18,000, but it is still a $20,000 roof that the owner pays the first $2,000 of [t6BiCluK7GY @ 00:01:12]. State Restoration Services repeats the math with a $25,000 roof and $5,000 deductible netting $20,000, adding that carriers sometimes split that $20,000 into 50/50 payments, half now and half after the build, and that no insurer will ever ask the owner to mail them the deductible [06ChGuOZCto @ 00:00:23]. Chad Michael closes the confusion at the kitchen table with a medical copay script: a $50 copay on a $1,000 doctor bill goes to the doctor, the insurer pays the other $950, and the contractor is the doctor in that picture [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:26:09]. Chad says owners who insist they already paid the deductible because it came out of the check usually get it once the copay frame lands.

The second consensus is blunt: a contractor who waives the deductible is either lying to the carrier or stealing from the roof. Anne Pullen calls a waiver offer a request to commit insurance fraud, straight up, and says the contractor who makes the deductible disappear is usually planning to inflate the estimate to absorb it, which is fraud with the homeowner's name on the paperwork and illegal in most states [tLwSSUZ6Awc @ 00:01:39]. Brent Simmons answers the same question with '100% yes, it is illegal,' and warns that the waived $2,000 is coming from somewhere, usually the quality of the roof [t6BiCluK7GY @ 00:01:46]. Chad Michael spells out the paperwork trick: on a $20,000 estimate with a $1,000 deductible, an honest invoice of $19,000 would just drop the carrier's payment to $18,000, so waivers only work when the contractor tells the insurer they charged $20,000, which Chad calls a felony no matter which state you are in [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:32:12]. Chad also needles the Facebook crowd of 'perfect' contractors who claim every client writes them a deductible check, saying that simply does not happen once you understand the competitive nature of storm work, and that clients chase waivers because everybody else is doing it [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:24:46].

Practitioners also agree the deductible owners think they have is often not the one that applies. Anne Pullen flags percentage deductibles tied to the dwelling limit, not the damage: 2% on a $500,000 dwelling is $10,000, owed the same on a $12,000 loss or a total loss, and many policies stack a second, higher percentage that only fires for wind, hail, hurricane or wildfire [tLwSSUZ6Awc @ 00:00:55]. The Deductible channel runs the same trap on a $400,000 house at 2%, an $8,000 deductible against a $12,000 hail repair that leaves insurance paying $4,000, then warns wind and hail riders can hit 5%, or $20,000 before the carrier pays a cent [A4K6Yt2bnWk @ 00:07:12]. That channel also hammers that car and home deductibles are per claim with no yearly bucket, so March and June losses mean two separate deductibles [A4K6Yt2bnWk @ 00:01:15]. Adjuster TV frames the mandatory 1% or 3% wind and hail deductible as the price of living where everyone gets a new roof every summer, and says the deductible should be applied last, after RCV, depreciation and policy limits [zOFPOUrXGw4 @ 00:03:57]. Anne's operating rule: have the deductible and any down payment liquid before crews get scheduled, not tied up somewhere else and not waiting on the first insurance check.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: When the lender's name is on the check, the practitioners run a paperwork machine. Garrett Eriksson of Integrity Roofing and Painting, whose shop does about 97% of its work through insurance claims, tells owners to call the local branch first; the lucky version is walking in and getting the check endorsed, the hard version demands the contractor's license or insurance, a W-9, a signed lien waiver, the insurance scope and a contract whose price matches the claim estimate [Mi6XZq4h6yo @ 00:01:07]. Garrett adds that lenders may ask for a draw schedule and hold back a final payment until the owner calls for the lender's inspector after the roof is done [Mi6XZq4h6yo @ 00:02:53]. Richard Levisee of Acumen Contracting routes everything through the lender's loss draft department and reports one package that releases claims under $10,000 with no holdback, while claims over $10,000 trigger inspections, including a 50% inspection that roofs and gutters skip because they finish in one to two days [VFWDHse67ws @ 00:06:48]. Richard's speed hacks: overnight, fax and email the identical packet so one misplaced sheet cannot stall the claim, and file a third party authorization so they can chase the lender every three days, because lenders never call when something is missing [VFWDHse67ws @ 00:08:05].

Chad Michael treats the deductible problem as an opportunity rather than a reason to lie. The engine is ACV-only coverage: other structures such as fences, sheds and playgrounds often carry non-recoverable depreciation, marked by brackets instead of parentheses, and Chad learned that the hard way on an ACV bed-and-breakfast job, doing all the decking and framing and absorbing the shortfall [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:23:30]. Flip it around and the same fence line becomes deductible money: if the owner skips that ACV work, Chad says the client goes from $1,798 short to $1,307 ahead, usually paid on a separate check that can be signed straight over to the contractor, and Chad tells the adjuster exactly what they did with it [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:27:55]. When no ACV money exists, Chad's last-resort move is hiring the owner as a subcontractor for a trade such as painting; the owner still pays the full deductible and turns over all insurance proceeds, and the subcontract is kept as a separate transaction [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:30:48]. Chad calls this creative financing, raised as a matter of course through a two-to-three-hour inspection of every room, closet and elevation. State Restoration Services sells the same promise in plainer terms, saying it is not waiving or rebating the deductible, yet 99% of the time the owner gets a new roof and pays absolutely nothing [06ChGuOZCto @ 00:01:16].

Two filters decide whether a claim or a refund is worth chasing. The Deductible channel runs the fender-bender math: a $900 repair against a $500 deductible pays $400, but a 30% at-fault surcharge on a $2,000-a-year policy adds $600 a year, $1,800 over three years, so filing costs $2,300 versus $900 cash [A4K6Yt2bnWk @ 00:02:59]. The rule of thumb attributed to claims adjusters is to run the numbers on own-car repairs under about $1,500 and to file every time on five-figure losses, totals, injuries or anyone else's property [A4K6Yt2bnWk @ 00:04:29]. On refunds, Collision Crash Course reports paying the deductible to the shop after an underinsured motorist hit them, then getting it back through subrogation about six months later [jcrOa0gm--g @ 00:01:54]. State Farm says the refund can take several months or years, may be prorated by liability share or limited by what is recovered, and can run through arbitration when a major insurer is involved; owners can also chase the deductible directly from the at-fault party if they tell State Farm and state in any release that they do not represent State Farm [bNL46sw5_5c @ 00:01:50]. The Deductible adds that the surcharge clock usually starts at payout, so file once for the full damage rather than twice for small stuff.

callout.title: Moves the field operators use to protect the check and the scope
callout.body: These are the specific plays practitioners run to keep the adjuster, the lender, and the contract working in the contractor's favor.
items: Never hand the adjuster your estimate at the meeting; tell them you were hired to perform all repairs they prescribe and you are there for your marching orders, so they show their cards first [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — DmesIP8hcak @ 00:39:21].

When your number is far from theirs, send an Xactimate photo report with no line items instead of the estimate; Chad's ran 172 pages with two photos each to force a reinspection aimed at full siding replacement [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — DmesIP8hcak @ 00:41:19].

Write the lender contract precisely, because a vague contract leaves the mortgage claim handler to interpret what is owed and stalls the money in a communication breakdown [Richard Levisee — VFWDHse67ws @ 00:03:44].

Put the contract price on the insurance contract so it matches the price on the insurance claim estimate, letting that contract double as the contractor's estimate for the lender [Integrity Roofing and Painting — Mi6XZq4h6yo @ 00:02:21].

sop_steps.title: Lock the deductible number at signing
sop_steps.action: Pull the declarations page, find the percentage and any wind and hail deductible, then run the copay script.
sop_steps.detail: Find the deductible percentage and whether a separate wind and hail one exists, about 10 seconds of scrolling [The Deductible — A4K6Yt2bnWk @ 00:07:41], then explain it as the $50 copay paid to the doctor [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — DmesIP8hcak @ 00:26:09].

sop_steps.title: Hunt legal deductible money in the estimate
sop_steps.action: Flag bracketed non-recoverable ACV items on other structures and route that separate check to the deductible.
sop_steps.detail: If the owner skips the ACV fence work, the separate check can be signed over to cover the deductible, and the adjuster can be told openly [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — DmesIP8hcak @ 00:27:55].

sop_steps.title: Build and triple-send the lender package
sop_steps.action: Assemble W-9, lien waiver, license or insurance, scope, and matching contract; send by overnight, fax, and email.
sop_steps.detail: Lenders ask for the W-9, signed lien waiver and contract matching the claim price [Integrity Roofing and Painting — Mi6XZq4h6yo @ 00:01:07]; send all three ways so nothing gets lost [Richard Levisee — VFWDHse67ws @ 00:06:04].

sop_steps.title: Chase the release and final inspection
sop_steps.action: File a third party authorization, follow up every three days, and call for inspection the day the roof is done.
sop_steps.detail: Call the lender as soon as the roof is complete for their inspector [Integrity Roofing and Painting — Mi6XZq4h6yo @ 00:02:53] and follow up every three days because lenders never flag missing items [Richard Levisee — VFWDHse67ws @ 00:08:05].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split on this desk is what a contractor does about the homeowner's deductible. Anne Pullen opens flat: a contractor offering to cover or waive the deductible is asking the homeowner to commit insurance fraud, and the usual method is inflating the estimate to absorb it [tLwSSUZ6Awc @ 00:00:00]. Brent Simmons of Restoration Roofing calls waiving it 100 percent illegal, compares it to a doctor's copay nobody ever forgives, and warns that the missing $2,000 on a $20,000 roof comes out of roof quality [t6BiCluK7GY @ 00:01:46]. State Restoration Services sells the opposite outcome without the illegal method: the pitch is pulling enough money from the carrier that the homeowner pays absolutely nothing, which the speaker says works 99 percent of the time, while insisting it is not waiving the deductible and not cash back [06ChGuOZCto @ 00:01:16]. Chad Michael sits in the middle. Chad mocks the Facebook contractors who claim every client writes a deductible check, saying it just does not happen, and draws the felony line only at lying to the carrier about the billed amount [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:24:25]. Chad's legal workaround is hunting non-recoverable ACV money, such as a fence the owner may never repair, and signing that separate check over toward the deductible, then telling the adjuster exactly what was done [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:27:37].

Assignment of benefits splits the room by vantage point. Timothy Ankle of Butler Legal, counseling carriers in Florida, lays out the contractor's logic: the executed AOB gives the contractor confidence of payment because the claim goes straight to the insurer, and Florida law holds that a policy's anti-assignment clause does not block post-loss assignment of benefits [rxahzd6qaCw @ 00:01:32]. Crossroads Insurance Recovery concedes AOB at first looked like a good idea after Hurricanes Florence and Michael, since destroyed properties could not reliably receive mail or money, then reports contractors began walking off half-started jobs or doing hasty shoddy work once the money was locked in [iKLGuESx4po @ 00:01:10]. Holmes Drafting Services, speaking from the agency side, calls AOB a four-letter word and walks the worst case: the roofer bills a $100,000 roof, the carrier values the shingle roof at $20,000, and the roofer liens the house for the $80,000 gap and sues the carrier [zzzZPeokDUk @ 00:01:10]. WFTV's Action 9 segment shows the political fight: regulators and the Florida Chamber blame inflated AOB claims for rate hikes, cite a $40,000 claim on a 500-square-foot home after a water leak, and note trial lawyers backing AOB contracts against a reform bill requiring written itemized estimates before any work [DS9xGSJEQ-k @ 00:01:39].

On not-at-fault losses, practitioners offer two routes with different cash timing. Collision Crash Course says claiming against the at-fault party's policy means no deductible out of pocket, while opening the claim on your own policy means paying the shop the deductible and waiting on subrogation; the host's own refund after an underinsured-motorist hit took about six months [jcrOa0gm--g @ 00:01:54]. State Farm frames the refund as some or all of the deductible, scaled by your share of liability or by whether the recovery equals the deductible, warns subrogation can run months or years through arbitration or litigation, and says it may chase an uninsured responsible party too, though that is not always successful [bNL46sw5_5c @ 00:00:47]. On mortgage-named checks, the two contractors run different playbooks. Garrett Eriksson of Integrity Roofing and Painting starts by calling the local branch, where endorsement can be a simple walk-in, and builds the packet around an insurance contract whose price matches the claim estimate [Mi6XZq4h6yo @ 00:00:33]. Richard Levisee goes heavier: a third-party authorization so the contractor works the loss draft department directly, the packet sent by overnight, fax, and email at once, and follow-up calls about every three days because the servicer will never call to say something is missing [VFWDHse67ws @ 00:07:52].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest firsthand loss on record is Chad Michael's ACV trap. Other structures like fences, sheds, and playgrounds often pay actual cash value only, with non-recoverable depreciation shown in brackets; a contractor who misses that agrees to all prescribed repairs for nothing but the deductible, finishes, and discovers the client is short $1,798 with no money left [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:22:49]. The client says the contractor was the expert and refuses to pay, so the contractor eats it, as Chad did on a bed-and-breakfast job with all the decking and framing, saying they about died after that one [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:23:17]. The second leak is Xactimate's default removal trade. Removal lines default to DMO general demolition labor instead of RFG roofing at roughly one third the price, and the same default runs through drywall, siding, and carpet; Chad's team documented every change with screenshots and notes and struck out on all twenty estimates they tried [DmesIP8hcak @ 00:16:40]. Chad blames speed economics: adjusters paid on job scale get estimates kicked back, learn to strip items, and know that almost nobody files supplements. Butler Legal flags the water-side version, where assigned leakage or seepage claims get fought because the contractor often finished all the work before first notice of loss [rxahzd6qaCw @ 00:22:02].

Homeowner traps start with the deductible math nobody runs. Anne Pullen warns that a 2 percent deductible on a $500,000 dwelling limit is $10,000 owed whether the loss is $12,000 or total, that a second higher wind, hail, hurricane, or wildfire deductible may apply, and that the money is usually due before crews are even scheduled [tLwSSUZ6Awc @ 00:00:55]. The Deductible runs the same shock on a $400,000 house: 2 percent means $8,000, so a $12,000 hail roof nets the owner just $4,000 from the carrier, and a separate wind-hail deductible up to 5 percent means $20,000 before the insurer pays a cent [A4K6Yt2bnWk @ 00:07:12]. The same channel shows the small-claim trap on autos: a $900 repair against a $500 deductible draws a $400 check, but an at-fault surcharge of 20 to 40 percent lasting 3 to 5 years pushes total cost to $2,300 versus $900 paid in cash; worse, handing $500 cash to keep a bumper tap off the record leaves you personally on the hook when the other driver's neck hurts two weeks later [A4K6Yt2bnWk @ 00:06:14]. Collision Crash Course adds the cash-flow check: a not-at-fault refund through subrogation took about six months, so budget around it [jcrOa0gm--g @ 00:02:11].

Assignment and paperwork failures are where claims stall or die. Holmes Drafting Services names the AOB worst case outright: an open claim on your policy, a lien on your house, and a lawsuit against your carrier, all at once [zzzZPeokDUk @ 00:01:29]. Crossroads Insurance Recovery adds that once the AOB is signed, the named insured is cut out of payment and cannot redirect a botched job to another contractor, while the mortgage company that still wants its monthly payments has lost its repair-account control; contractors focused on bricks and sticks also know nothing about additional living expense money for hotels, meals, and mileage [iKLGuESx4po @ 00:03:42]. Butler Legal reports the drafting traps that sink assignments: a direction to pay mistaken for a true AOB, one spouse signing for a home held by the entirety, and conditional assignments where the work is not yet done [rxahzd6qaCw @ 00:08:01]. On mortgage checks, Richard Levisee warns that a vague contract leaves a servicer's claim handler to interpret the amounts, that one misplaced sheet can freeze the whole claim, and that claims over $10,000 at the sample servicer trigger an inspection process before money moves [VFWDHse67ws @ 00:03:59].

callout.title: Four Checks Before Money or Signatures Move
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, stall, or legal trap a practitioner hit or watched happen on a live claim.
items: Before agreeing to a deductible-only scope, pull which coverages are ACV only with bracketed non-recoverable depreciation, or expect to eat the shortfall [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — DmesIP8hcak @ 00:22:33].
Kill any deductible deal that requires billing the carrier a number the client was never charged; Chad calls that a felony in every state [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — DmesIP8hcak @ 00:32:12].
Before relying on an AOB, confirm it is a true assignment and not a direction to pay, and that every named insured signed it [Butler Legal — rxahzd6qaCw @ 00:06:17].
Before submitting a mortgage packet, make the contract precise enough that no servicer claim handler has to guess the amounts or scope [Richard Levisee — VFWDHse67ws @ 00:03:44].

chapters.pull_quote: "The way people get around that is they lie to an insurance company, which is a felony no matter which state you're in." — Chad Michael - The Practitioner (DmesIP8hcak @ 00:32:12).
action_checklist: Pull the declarations page and find the deductible percentage plus any separate wind and hail deductible before the next storm [The Deductible — A4K6Yt2bnWk @ 00:07:41].
At signing, explain the deductible as a $50 copay paid to the doctor on a $1,000 bill so the client stops saying it was already paid [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — DmesIP8hcak @ 00:26:09].
When the gap is huge, send the carrier a photo report instead of the full estimate to trigger a reinspection without showing your cards [Chad Michael - The Practitioner — DmesIP8hcak @ 00:40:44].
When the check names a mortgage company, call the loss draft department to open the claim and get the required package [Richard Levisee — VFWDHse67ws @ 00:01:18].
Call the mortgage company as soon as the roof replacement is complete so its inspector clears release of the final check [Integrity Roofing and Painting — Mi6XZq4h6yo @ 00:02:37].
If chasing a deductible directly from the at-fault party, notify your insurer and tell the other party you do not represent it in any release [State Farm Insurance — bNL46sw5_5c @ 00:01:50].

chapters.question_prompt: How do storm roofing contractors inspect hail damage, write roof estimates, sell hail jobs, and price and pay crews profitably?
chapters.title: Storm Roofing: Hail Inspections, Roof Estimates, and Crew Economics
chapters.subtitle: Insurance restoration roofing basics, hail reports, homeowner hail checks, TPO and commercial hail inspections and coatings, the hail sales process, hail claim and roof repair estimates in Xactimate X1, paying and managing subcontractors, and pricing roofs for profit
chapters.executive_summary: Storm roofing operators across adjusting, sales, and crew management converge on one rule: the evidence wins the roof. Adjuster TV's Matt shoots 90 to 120 photos per claim and walks every elevation in the same order, while Chris Zimmerman calls proof that replacement beats repair the linchpin of restoration sales. On the estimate, Xactimate macros, 10 to 15 percent waste, age-over-lifespan depreciation, and a hard self-check drive clean files; Claim Daddy's Haag-based worksheet prices repair at $24.80 per shingle against $368.78 per square. Crew economics are blunt: Adam Bensman targets $250 to $450 per square and calls $190 unprofitable, RoofCoach prices by dividing cost by 0.65, and ProLine warns that 54 percent markup is only 35 percent margin. Disagreements center on waste factors, O&P, 1099 labor, and coating-versus-tear-off commercial strategy.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who touches a hail roof agrees that documentation, not opinion, moves money. Adjuster TV's Matt, a CAT adjuster since 1999, walks every house front, right, back, left on every file [6084H_VeZTA @ 00:40:37], then shoots roughly 30 to 50 roof photos and 90 to 120 photos total; that photo set later refuted a roofer who ripped shingles off after the inspection. Matt also says no-damage findings demand even more proof than paid ones. Chris Zimmerman frames the same principle from the sales side: the linchpin of restoration roofing is evidence that replacement, not repair, is necessary, because insurers 'generally speaking don't want to pay' [1quXRyfkTgo @ 00:04:12]. Homeowner Explained pushes owners to build the file themselves: photograph soft metals and AC fins, check downspouts for granules, use a coin for scale, turn on date stamps, and save the weather report [MPSOkm3YFak @ 00:03:35]. On commercial work, RestoreMasters' Kevin reports that the formal walkthrough and claim reports at West Georgia Technical College uncovered more damage than either the crew or the client expected, including a damaged pipe, dinged metal siding, windows, doors, and skylight-driven interior damage, all of which had to be returned to pre-loss condition [lkJlJQH7bVw @ 00:01:58]. The working rule across all four: if it is not photographed, measured, and written down, it does not get paid.

The practitioners also agree on what real hail damage looks like, and what it does not. Claim Daddy teaches that genuine hail bruises the shingle mat, while pulverized granules, quarter-shaped gouges, and non-random field hits point to mechanical damage, and that a contractor damaging a roof leaves a non-random pattern that gives the game away [yytgxtBGSF8 @ 00:30:46]. Matt draws a hard line on masonry: 'ice is not harder than rock,' so brick is never paid as hail no matter how big the ice balls were [6084H_VeZTA @ 00:43:04]. On TPO, the damage hides. RestoreMasters' John McDonald reads hail splatter for volume, density, and direction, feels for indentations at large-splatter spots, then cuts into and peels back the membrane; impact dents in the ISO board mean it is compromised and must be replaced [rw8dEal_Ppk @ 00:00:42]. Kevin's crew at LaGrange found hail holes so numerous and small that 'that's why we have to get up on personal with these things,' because the dirty, weathered membrane hides them from a casual walk [lkJlJQH7bVw @ 00:00:40]. The shared standard is that the inspector's eyes get within inches of the surface, whether on a residential slope or a commercial deck, and that splatter, soft metals, and AC fins establish that a storm actually hit the property before anyone argues scope or price.

The third point of agreement is how storm money actually moves, and it is never one check. Matt explains ACV to homeowners as 'used car value,' holding back roughly 10% on a three-year-old 30-year shingle, and his F9 script tells the insured that withheld depreciation, such as 40% on a 10-year-old roof with a 25-year lifespan, is released once they send the final contractor bill [ccWMQpIzp_w @ 00:04:49]. Chris Zimmerman lays out the same chain from the contractor seat: a certificate of completion releases withheld depreciation, the lender may have to sign the check, and payment lands 30 to 60 days after completion [1quXRyfkTgo @ 00:02:47]. Homeowner Explained adds the deductible reality: wind/hail deductibles run 1 to 5%, so 2% on a $300,000 home is $6,000, and 'if your damage is less than that, filing won't pay you anything' [MPSOkm3YFak @ 00:05:04]. Claim Daddy's training file applies 1% of $450,000 for a $4,500 deductible and notes southern wind/hail deductibles commonly sit at 1 to 2% [yytgxtBGSF8 @ 00:11:49]. Anyone selling, building, or adjusting storm roofs has to know the deductible, the ACV/RCV split, and the recoverable depreciation path before quoting a homeowner a single number, or the deal collapses at the kitchen table.
